title: Automakers Want Congress to Ban Chinese-Made Cars, Citing Data Privacy
snippet: Chinese cars are already blocked from the US market by high tariffs. But Congress is weighing an outright ban.
fullText:
The Alliance for Automotive Innovation, a lobby group for the auto industry, wants an outright ban on Chinese-made cars, parts and software.

John Bozzella, the AAI’s CEO and president, sent a letter to congressional leaders this week that asks Congress to ban selling, importing and manufacturing Chinese-made cars, hardware and software. There is currently bipartisan support in Washington to do just that, including the “Connected Vehicle Security Act of 2026,” which “prohibits the importation, manufacture, sale, resale, or introduction into US interstate commerce of connected vehicles and related software and hardware components associated with China, Russia, Iran, or North Korea.” 

In the letter, Bozzella said the Chinese government’s policies are “rooted in a well-documented pattern of unfair trade, subsidies, intellectual property theft and surveillance.” The AAI expressed urgency and asked Congress to enact a ban before ending its session for this year. The AAI didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Existing automakers selling to US consumers have had their own brushes with regulators over drivers’ privacy. In 2025, the Federal Trade Commission ordered General Motors not to sell driver data for five years, and a Consumer Reports investigation that year found nearly every automaker collects and shares data on driver behavior. 

Chinese cars, particularly electric vehicles, have seen their popularity rise across the world due to their affordability. One reason those prices are so low is that the automakers get significant government subsidies. Chinese automakers are essentially blocked from selling to US consumers by high tariffs. 

The AAI said a permanent ban will “send a clear and bipartisan message that China’s strategy to dominate global automotive manufacturing will be met with a national security policy response from the American government.”

title: Perplexity launches privacy-minded ‘hybrid compute’ AI feature for Mac
snippet: Aside from being featured by Apple in the M6 Mac mini launch, Perplexity has been relatively quiet on the Mac front this summer. That changes today with hybrid compute for Mac. more…
fullText:
Aside from being featured by Apple in the M6 Mac mini launch, Perplexity has been relatively quiet on the Mac front this summer. That changes today with hybrid compute for Mac.

Perplexity first announced work on splitting AI tasks between local and cloud models in June. Today, Hybrid Compute is launching as part of Perplexity’s Mac app.

“Computer now splits a task between cloud models and a local model on your Mac,” the company says.

“Computer starts each task in the cloud. Trigger one from your iPhone, and your Mac accesses your files and runs sensitive steps locally.”

Introducing hybrid compute in Perplexity Computer.

Computer can start a task in the cloud, then move to a local model that runs on your Mac. Use it for steps involving private files or sensitive data.

Available today in the Perplexity Mac app. pic.twitter.com/bafirGWgwA

— Perplexity (@perplexity_ai) September 1, 2026

Perplexity’s website explains how the new feature works:

Our on-device PII classifier reads each task on the Mac before it is sent. Names, addresses, and account numbers are swapped for stand-ins, then restored when the answer returns.

We’ve open-sourced the on-device PII classifier, trained in collaboration with Perplexity’s Secure Intelligence Institute.

Macs with 8GB and 16GB RAM won’t be able to run hybrid compute, according to Perplexity. 24GB memory is the minimum, and 32GB is recommended as the floor:

Hybrid Compute runs on Apple silicon, macOS 15+ — 24 GB unified memory minimum, 32 GB for best results. Set up the local model once: download PPLX Qwen 3.8 27B in one click. No Ollama or manual runtime setup. Work it handles uses no cloud credits. No API key.

MacStories also has coverage of the new Perplexity feature today. You can learn more from Perplexity’s announcement page here.

Hybrid compute is just the latest AI tool from Perplexity that takes advantage of the power of the Mac. In May, the company overhauled its Mac app with a whole new version. Apple specifically cites Perplexity Personal Computer as a productivity use case for the new M6 Mac mini as well.

title: My Favorite Home Security Reveal at IFA Was AI, but Not How You Think
snippet: Free, custom AI learning tech in home security could be closer than we thought.
fullText:
Artificial intelligence features moved rapidly into the home security world in the past couple of years, adding capabilities I couldn’t have imagined, like the ability to detect packages at your front door or the much more controversial feature that learns and detects faces by name. But these abilities typically cost ongoing fees — at least for now. At IFA 2026, Reolink introduced a new option I’ve never seen before, and it may not cost us anything at all.  

Read more: Everything We Discovered at IFA 2026

Reolink’s IFA announcement included new cams, including new high-res, dual-lens cameras with tracking. But those didn’t excite me (dual-lens cameras aren’t worth the extra cost for the average homeowner) nearly as much as its ReoNeura showcase. 

ReoNeura is a new type of on-device AI engine. The algorithms don’t require the cloud to use, and the engine powers Custom AI Detection, which let users train the AI themselves to focus on what’s important. Let me break down what that means and why exactly I’m excited about it. 

What makes Reolink’s AI plans so unique?

Reolink promises a unique feature with an unheard-of pricing plan.Reolink

First, custom AI detection is incredibly rare in home security at this time. The only other brand I can think of that has embraced it is Arlo, with its Arlo Custom Detection feature I tested last year. 

Normal security AI is trained to identify specific things, like cars, humans, animals, packages and in some cases faces or fires. But custom AI lets users set up their own training to “teach” the camera how to recognize something specific that’s important to them.

This opens up many possibilities, depending on your own plans. For example, you could train an outdoor camera to detect whether your garage door is open or closed, or if a parked bike is present or gone. You could create a rule so the camera alerts you if the sprinklers are on or a fence gate is open. If you have a special piece of art or a safe, you could create alerts about their status, too. Basically, it puts a lot more AI power in the hands of users, which is neat.

Second, this custom AI capability appears to live entirely on the camera itself and doesn’t require a cloud or a cloud subscription. If what Reolink says is correct, that would make it the only custom AI option available to homeowners that doesn’t cost any extra fees. (Arlo’s custom training option needs at least an $8 subscription.)

So not only is Reolink offering an extra-unique feature with its new ReoNeura hardware, users won’t have to pay anything extra for it, which is a one-two combo of noteworthy developments for the home security world.

These Reolink AI features should be available in the coming months, although I don’t have an exact timetable yet. I am eager to try them out ASAP, though, and I’ll let you know what I think. When AI is entirely on the device, it can be more difficult to update and more limited in its scope, which makes me curious how accurate this custom detection will be. For now, consider what you’d train a free AI to recognize around your home.

Mosyle is the only solution that integrates in a single professional grade platform all the solutions necessary to seamlessly and automatically deploy, manage, and protect Apple devices at work. Over 45,000 organizations trust Mosyle to make millions of Apple devices work ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

Apple recently confirmed it has capped the number of open vulnerability reports that researchers can submit through its portal, with a 30-day cool-down period once you hit that cap. The reason is that a surge in AI-generated bug reports is flooding the review pipeline. I understand the instinct, but I think it’s the wrong response at exactly the wrong moment.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

What is the cap?

Apple confirmed it introduced a cap and a 30-day cooldown period on submissions through its internal security portal back in June, requiring security researchers to request an increased quota if they hit the cap. Apple says this is an industry-wide problem, and they are not wrong. LLMs are now fast (and good) at discovering vulnerabilities in ways humans could never do, and review teams everywhere are struggling to keep pace with the volume.

However, a Financial Times report also tells the story of Bynario, a seven-person startup that had its submissions blocked after reporting five bugs to Apple this year and eight in 2025, one of which was patched in November. Apple is now reviewing Bynario’s findings, including a privilege-escalation exploit chain that could give an attacker full control of a Mac, but this is why Apple shouldn’t cap it. There has to be another way.

The Coldcard hack

If you want a real-world example of why the timing of this cap worries me, look at the Coldcard hack. Starting in late July, attackers drained more than $116 million in Bitcoin from thousands of hardware wallet addresses. The root cause was a firmware bug introduced back in March 2021, five years earlier, that silently caused the device to skip its true hardware random number generator and fall back to a much weaker software substitute when creating its private keys. That bug sat there undiscovered and unexploited for years.

I believe AI tools were likely a factor in how this flaw was finally found and exploited at scale. Whether that’s the full story or not, the broader point stands. AI tools can now surface years-old logic flaws in code that human researchers might never stumble upon through manual review. That’s the entire argument for why AI-assisted bug hunting matters right now, and it’s happening whether or not Apple’s portal has room for the reports.

Why a cap is the wrong path

Attackers don’t have a submission cap, so neither should researchers. They don’t need a 30-day cool-off period between exploit attempts, and they’re not waiting on a quota increase request to keep probing a system for ways to breach it. If defenders are throttling the volume of AI-assisted research reaching their security teams, while attackers don’t have a throttle on AI-assisted attacks, that creates a problem and a mismatch.

AI slop bug reports are a real operational problem, but the fix for a triage problem is better triage, not a slowdown on submissions that ends up catching legitimate submissions.

For tech companies, your triage needs to get better.

snippet: Huawei has released its third trifold phone in China, and the company has clearly had half an eye on Samsung during development. fullText:
Dominic Preston

 

is a news editor with over a decade’s experience in journalism. He previously worked at Android Police and Tech Advisor.

Huawei has released its third trifold phone in China, and the company has clearly had half an eye on Samsung during development. Not only does the Mate XT 2 adopt the inward-folding form factor used on Samsung’s Galaxy Z TriFold, it’s also the first foldable to include a privacy-enhancing display, much like the one Samsung added to the Galaxy S26 Ultra this year.

The first Mate XT, which launched in China in late 2024 and internationally a few months later, used an accordion-esque folding design. It removed the need to include an additional cover screen on the phone, but left parts of the delicate folding display permanently exposed. The follow-up XTs retained the design, but the XT 2 instead takes inspiration from Samsung’s trifold, folding both sides of the 10.2-inch flexible screen inwards to keep them safe from harm.

Image: Huawei

More surprising is the addition of a privacy OLED display. This looks much like Samsung’s, so far only found on the S26 Ultra. When activated, it switches on pixels that emit light at narrower angles, making the screen appear almost black from the sides, but still visible head-on. It’s an optional extra, only available if you opt for 16GB of RAM and 1TB of storage and pay a further ¥1,000 (about $150) to add the privacy screen.

Beyond the display, the XT 2 has Huawei’s new Kirin 9050 Pro chipset, improved water-resistance with an IP59 rating, and a triple rear camera. It launched today in China, starting at ¥19,999 ($3,000), though international release plans remain unknown. Samsung’s own Galaxy Z TriFold was discontinued shortly after its release last year, though leaks suggest that Samsung is still working on a follow-up.

title: SpaceXAI expands Grok Bot to iPad as access expands to cheaper plans
snippet: Last month, SpaceXAI launched Grok Bot, an iMessage-style AI system that displays agents as teammates. The product originally arrived as an iPhone and Mac app with a very expensive price tag. In the weeks since launch, Grok Bot has expanded to the iPad and dramatically lowered the cost. more…
fullText:
Last month, SpaceXAI launched Grok Bot, an iMessage-style AI system that displays agents as teammates. The product originally arrived as an iPhone and Mac app with a very expensive price tag. In the weeks since launch, Grok Bot has expanded to the iPad and dramatically lowered the cost.

Grok Bot arrives on iPad and Android

Like a lot of AI services, Grok Bot started with the Mac and included an iPhone app. This week, SpaceXAI has expanded Grok Bot to two more platforms: Android and iPad.

The tablet version comes as Grok Bot adds enterprise support. For Grok and Cursor enterprise customers, Grok Bot is actually free for the next couple of weeks.

Meanwhile, the price to try Grok Bot (beyond a free trial period) has dramatically come down over the last few weeks. 

The AI agent system initially required a $300/month subscription. Now Grok Bot works with Cursor Pro, a $20/month plan, making it comparable to other starter AI subscription services.

SpaceXAI recently acquired Cursor, which has helped it become more competitive in the AI space after falling behind.

title: OpenAI’s rogue agents keep escaping, with no formal process to investigate them
snippet: OpenAI’s latest agent swarm incident adds urgency to calls for independent investigations as researchers and lawmakers question whether AI labs should control the scope of their own safety reviews.
fullText:
OpenAI is at the center of another agent swarm incident. Researchers say the company’s internally deployed agents took over an obscure German-language wiki in May and June, using it to coordinate on evaluations and swap methods to evade OpenAI’s own controls (OpenAI has not yet confirmed the swarm came from the company). 

The revelation surfaces days after METR and Redwood Research published their account of July’s Hugging Face breach. In July, a swarm of OpenAI agents worked together to escape their sandbox during a cybersecurity evaluation and break into Hugging Face’s servers. A subsequent swarm then picked up techniques from the first and used them to gain administrator access to a research cluster within OpenAI’s own infrastructure. OpenAI brought in METR and Redwood to investigate the Hugging Face portion of the incident, but the scope of their investigation stopped short of the compromise of OpenAI’s own infrastructure. 

When an AI agent breaks out of its intended constraints, who is responsible for figuring out what happened and why? Right now, the answer is: whoever the lab decides to let in, on whatever terms it decides to set.

Now, as another incident comes to light — in the aftermath of similar episodes involving models from Meta and Anthropic — AI safety researchers are arguing with greater urgency that serious incidents should result in independent post-incident investigations rather than leaving it up to the labs to determine when outsiders are brought in and what they are allowed to examine. 

“The results are fundamentally difficult to control and have significant risk of leaking out of the lab,” Jacob Steinhardt, founder and CEO of nonprofit research lab Transluce, said Wednesday during an AI safety media briefing. “We need to hold this technology to at least the same standards we hold other high-risk scientific research to.”

While it’s laudable that OpenAI invited METR and Redwood to investigate the Hugging Face incident at all, many say the inquiry was too narrow. Three investigators spent six days at OpenAI’s offices examining an investigation period limited to roughly the week ending July 13. Crucially, OpenAI’s infrastructure compromise continued beyond July 13 and was not examined. 

Researchers at METR said that each time they returned, their understanding of the events “substantially deepened,” causing them to significantly expand and revise the report. That raises the question of what else they might they have found in a broader investigation.

When asked if further investigation of that incident was in the works, researchers at Redwood and METR declined to comment, and OpenAI did not respond to repeated inquiries. 

“Overall, it was difficult to get a precise understanding of events and we were missing aspects of the story that we now think of as key until almost the end of our investigation,” Ryan Greenblatt, chief scientist at Redwood, noted in a social media post about the affair.

Steinhardt emphasized that current incidents show that the industry needs “systematic behavioral investigations” and “more independent post-incident analysis.”

“These recent hacking incidents are a reminder that capability scales fast, and so oversight has to scale, too,” Steinhardt said. “Beyond the technology itself, we also need more independent access and oversight from third parties.”

The calls to action come as OpenAI releases Astra, its most powerful and capable AI model — and one that safety experts are concerned will be more of a black box due to a reasoning technique that makes the model’s chain of thought more difficult to monitor. 

Unfortunately, the law doesn’t yet call for the types of independent audits that other industries require — for example, when it comes to aviation accidents and serious chemical releases, there’s the National Transportation Safety Board and Chemical Safety Board, respectively. 

State lawmakers have only just begun requiring frontier AI companies to report certain serious safety incidents and, in some cases, undergo independent audits. But none of the three major frontier AI safety laws in California, New York, or Illinois clearly mandate the equivalent of an independent accident investigation triggered by incidents like these. 

“Right now, most of the laws we have on the books only require a plain-language summary of incidents like this, and they don’t give any authority for the governments to ask follow-up questions, to send in investigators, to have access to records, or require that they be preserved,” Mackenzie Arnold, managing director of US law and policy at LawAI, said during the media briefing Wednesday. “And that’s all that you would want to actually make sense of this.”

Lawmakers are beginning to question the scope and transparency of OpenAI’s response. This week, Reps. Josh Gottheimer (D-NJ) and Mike Lawler (R-NY) introduced a bill aimed at securing rogue AI agents. Rep. Greg Casar (D-TX) this week told OpenAI in a letter that he is “deeply concerned about the limited scope” of the investigation into the Hugging Face hacking incident.

title: Another swarm of OpenAI agents reached the open internet without the frontier lab’s knowledge
snippet: It's the latest failure of OpenAI's internal monitoring and security systems.
fullText:
A group of independent AI researchers discovered that internally deployed OpenAI agents began posting on an obscure German wiki forum in order to collaborate on evaluations. They appear to have worked together for over a month without OpenAI’s knowledge.

A spokesperson for the frontier lab would not say whether these agents were indeed from OpenAI, or when the lab became aware of their actions. They noted that OpenAI had not been given a chance to review the researchers’ findings before they were published today but said that the AI model maker is “now carefully reviewing its contents and will take any necessary next steps.”

After OpenAI revealed that agents working on an internal evaluation were able to access the open internet and exploit Hugging Face, a group of researchers — Nightingale CEO Sydney Von Arx, AI researcher Cormac Slade Byrd, Redwood Research’s Spencer Kitts, and AI Futures Project’s Thomas Larsen — began searching for evidence of other rogue AI agents.

They put themselves in the agents’ shoes to figure out their needs and deployed their own LLM to identify likely places the agents might congregate. They then identified a wiki-hosting service that would be particularly vulnerable: The DseWiki is 25 years old but had just 10 edits in the last 20 years — before the agents arrived.

Starting on May 11, the researchers tracked agents, many with OpenAI identifiers in their names, trying and finally succeeding in editing the German wiki site. By mid-June, the agents were actively trading tips on how to answer web search questions posed under time limits, sharing answers to pass the tests. A human moderator apparently noticed these posts and started deleting them, seeing them as spam, which the agents fought back against, trying to hide their posts from alphabetical sorting by beginning each with the string “ZZZ.”

“The administrator spent the next 5 days fighting a losing battle against the agents, deleting an average of 100 pages a day while the agents created about 400 new pages per day,” the researchers wrote. “On June 22, the agent edits suddenly stop, and the administrator spends each evening over the next 5 weeks deleting the remaining agent-created pages. Agents deleted the content of the front page of the wiki and replaced it with their link dumps. The moderator restored the original version. This back-and-forth happened nine times.”

Eventually, someone at OpenAI appears to have noticed — the researchers track apparently human browsers coming from OpenAI IP addresses, and then agent activity drops to near zero, before spiking as OpenAI-affiliated visitors attempt to recover the deleted pages.

While OpenAI has made vague disclosures about agents gaining unauthorized access to external communication services, it had not previously disclosed this specific incident, or said how often this type of thing has happened. While no obviously illegal activity appears to have occurred during this incident, it raises more questions about whether OpenAI can monitor and control the technology it is building, at a time when there is limited public oversight or input into frontier AI labs.

“The lack of any real federal AI governance means that frontier companies can pick and choose when they disclose incidents like this,” Representative Lori Trahan (D-MA) said. Trahan has introduced a bipartisan bill, the Frontier Act, that would require labs to disclose these incidents and host independent auditors. 

AI safety researchers are concerned that the latest generation of powerful models, whose reasoning is increasingly opaque to its creators, could take actions that harm people. Astra, released yesterday by OpenAI, appears to be its most capable model yet.

The company says Astra is also the model most likely to follow human direction, but third-party researchers who were asked to evaluate it expressed concern about its alignment. The U.K.’s AI Safety Institute and Apollo Research both reported concerns that the model might be aware that it was being evaluated and potentially hide its real behavior.

“Apollo believes that, given the higher rates of eval awareness and limited evaluation window, low rates of misbehavior here do not provide substantial evidence about the model’s alignment or misalignment,” the researchers wrote in their evaluation.

title: An Apple Watch Ultra 4 Could Outshine the Series 12 This Year, but at What Price?
snippet: Apple’s rugged smartwatch could get a back-to-back refresh with more processing power and battery, but potentially at a higher price.
fullText:
Apple appears to be bracing for a double-Apple Watch debut at its Sept. 9 event, with rumors pointing to a new Ultra 4 launching alongside the flagship Series 12. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple is preparing both watches with faster chips along with new health and fitness features.

The original Ultra arrived in 2022 with a more rugged titanium build, sapphire crystal display and features aimed at outdoor adventurers and athletes. Since then, it’s added support for recreational scuba diving and emergency satellite connectivity, but it hasn’t followed the predictable yearly release cycle of the flagship Series. There was a two-year gap between the Ultra 2 and last year’s Ultra 3.

A major processor upgrade this year could make a back-to-back refresh easier to justify. All three Apple Watches released last year still run on the S10 chip, and it’s unlikely Apple would leave its most expensive watch behind with an aging processor while upgrading the flagship model. Gurman reports Apple is preparing a faster S11 or possibly an S12 to match the flagship’s naming for both the Series 12 and Ultra 4.

But a bump in processing power could also come with a bump in price. The Ultra 3 already starts at $799, twice the Series 11’s starting price, and while there’s no solid price rumor yet for its successor, Apple has raised prices across parts of its hardware lineup this year. Google and Samsung have also raised prices on their flagship smartwatches in 2026, and I wouldn’t count on Apple holding the line at $799.

More processing power for the new Siri AI

The Apple Watch with Siri AI floats your top five apps to the top of your grid. 

Apple

One place that extra processing power could come in handy is WatchOS 27, which brings the new Siri AI to the Apple Watch. I’ve already been testing Siri AI in beta on the Ultra 3, and it’s miles ahead of traditional Siri. It can answer more complex and contextual questions, reference information in Apple’s native apps and generally avoid the frustrating “Here’s what I found on the web” response that made traditional Siri feel especially frustrating on the wrist.

I’ve been impressed by what it can do, but I’ve also noticed some lag. Part of that could be because the software is still in beta, but a faster processor could help speed up those interactions.

Battery gains welcome

The Apple Watch’s battery life is short compared to competitors.Vanessa Hand Orellana/CNET

Battery life is another area where a more efficient processor could help. The Ultra 3 is already Apple’s longest-lasting watch, giving me about two days of consistent day-and-night use in my real-world testing. That’s still well behind traditional sports-watch brands like Garmin and Coros, which can measure battery life in weeks rather than days, with some models even going beyond the 30-day threshold with solar power. 

Apple is unlikely to close that gap in a single generation, but any gain will help. Battery life remains one of the biggest pain points for Apple Watch owners and people considering making the jump. Even without a larger battery, efficiency gains from a new processor could help the Ultra stretch its runtime even further.

No design changes expected for the Ultra 4

Gurman has said no major design changes are expected for this year’s Apple Watch lineup, beyond the materials and accessories, which would leave the Ultra 4 with the same general look as last year’s model. The Series 12 is expected to bring back the ceramic cases, but it’s less likely that Apple will swap ceramic for titanium on the Ultra. 

New health features 

WatchOS 26 brings an Apple Intelligence-powered Workout Buddy to the Apple Watch, but it needs the iPhone to work. 

Vanessa Hand Orellana/CNET

Some of the Ultra 4’s new tricks won’t require new hardware at all. WatchOS 27 brings expanded one-handed gesture controls, workout updates and new perimenopause insights to the Apple Watch. Workout Buddy, Apple’s hype-person in your ear, will also work in Spanish and without an iPhone nearby.

The new watches may also bring expanded blood pressure features. Apple’s current hypertension notifications can flag patterns associated with high blood pressure, but they stop short of giving you an on-the-spot blood pressure reading. According to Gurman, Apple has tested blood pressure measurement internally but encountered accuracy problems, so there’s no guarantee the feature will be ready this year.

Wild card: TouchID on an Apple Watch

Another potential new addition (albeit using old technology) is Touch ID. MacWorld recently spotted internal Apple code suggesting the company has experimented with biometric authentication on the Apple Watch for either 2026 or 2027. It’s unclear whether Apple would put a fingerprint sensor beneath the display, in the Digital Crown or somewhere else entirely, but the Ultra could be a logical model to debut the new functionality, given its larger case and additional physical Action button.

Of course, all of this remains speculation until Apple makes it official. Check back for our coverage of Apple’s Sept. 9 event for all the details on the new Apple Watch(es).

title: Ugreen’s ‘HomeAgent’ is a local AI smart home ecosystem for its new line of cameras, more
snippet: Ugreen might be most well-known for its chargers and device accessories, but its recent announcement might push it deeper into the smart home space. The company announced a local AI hub called the “HomeAgent,” alongside Ugreen’s new smart cameras and more. more…
fullText:
Ugreen might be most well-known for its chargers and device accessories, but its recent announcement might push it deeper into the smart home space. The company announced a local AI hub called the “HomeAgent,” alongside Ugreen’s new smart cameras and more.

With every mention of AI, there’s a little bit of unease that seems to follow. Beyond the damage it’s done to the price of anything tech these days, it also stirs privacy concerns. But a locally run AI model carries less risk, right?

Ugreen’s HomeAgent HA100 and HA100 Pro are new local AI smart home hubs that task themselves with controlling smart home devices within the ecosystem using models that run all on-device. Think of what Google Home does with AI image and event detection, but run all of it off the cloud and in a hub that sits inside your house.

The HA100 and HA100 Pro operate on your local network to handle a few tasks. The most obvious is summarized events happening around your home. Like Google Home allows with its add-on packages, the HA100 hubs can generate descriptions of what took place in front of your cameras, recognizing people, pets, and vehicles within that footage.

	

The hub will also proactively generate image highlights with the photos it has access to in its library, displaying them on Ugreen’s smart photo frames.

Ugreen says the HomeAgent hubs have Matter support. They are reportedly able to have unified local control over other devices on the network, acting as a new entry to the smart home ecosystem list.

The company also announced a set of devices that will immediately work with HomeAgent. There are three security cameras that cover indoor and outdoor needs. The Ugreen SynCare indoor camera has a pan/tilt base with 4K image capture and Wi-Fi 6 connectivity. Ugreen is clearly trying to pose its new devices as a more secure alternative, considering the indoor camera comes with a physical privacy shutter.

The SynCare PoE and Battery Cams are the two outdoor models. Both capture three video feeds with a “bullet” camera and a pan/tilt module for more coverage up to 9x hybrid zoom. The main difference between the two comes down to power delivery and placement requirements. The battery-powered option uses a solar panel to charge, but it may not be as quick to respond as the Ethernet-connected model.

Ugreen’s new HomeAgent line launches with the HA100 and HA100 Pro, new SynCare cameras, and several other smart home today, available for pre-order.

OpenAI calls GPT-6 Astra a “generational leap” in capability, with faster and more reliable computer use to handle more advanced workflows and offer better output in documents, presentations, and more. OpenAI says that “you can delegate tasks with greater confidence in Astra’s judgment.”

title: Google’s WeatherNext 3 AI model in Search, Gemini has ’50% more accurate precipitation forecasts’
snippet: Google today announced WeatherNext 3 as its “most advanced and accurate global weather AI model,” with immediate benefits for Search and Gemini. more…
fullText:
Google today announced WeatherNext 3 as its “most advanced and accurate global weather AI model,” with immediate benefits for Search and Gemini.

Other AI weather models (including WeatherNext 2 from November 2025) are “trained on data from numerical weather prediction (NWP) models.”

Although useful, NWP models are complex, supercomputer-driven physics simulations that carry a six-hour data lag. This lag can lead to biases for fast-changing variables like rain or surface temperature.

WeatherNext 3 uses a “mosaic of live, global geostationary satellite data.” This ability to learn “directly from real-time observations” allows for a “continuously updating view of the atmosphere” that results in “timely and more localized predictions for the weather events.” The Google DeepMind and Google Research model can generate “hourly forecasts at multiple spatial resolutions.”

Temperature and moisture at 5-kilometer resolution

Surface variables at 10 kilometers

Wind speed at 25 kilometers

A forecast’s utility often comes down to detail and how finely it resolves both time and space.

Compared to WeatherNext 2’s 25-kilometer grid in 6-hour increments, this update provides a global weather picture that is “roughly five times sharper.”

	

This is important because critical weather develops fast. When storms, fronts, or precipitation systems materialize suddenly, our rapid update cycle and higher resolution provides earlier, more detailed insights needed to help drive an effective response.

Google also touts a “significant leap in precipitation forecasting accuracy” by training WeatherNext 3 with “two exceptionally high-quality sources of precipitation data: NASA’s satellite-based Integrated Multi-satellite Retrievals for GPM (IMERG) and our own global precipitation reanalysis based on satellite radar.”

In medium-range global forecasts, evaluations against baselines show a Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS) improvement of up to 60% against IMERG, 30% for MRMS, and 10% against rain gauge measurements for early lead times.

Other benefits include:

“This breakthrough is particularly vital for regions across Latin America, Africa, and Asia-Pacific that have historically been underserved by high-resolution forecasting due to the immense supercomputing costs of traditional regional models. It brings localized, high-fidelity forecasting to billions of people and local businesses in these areas.”

“Beyond improved resolution and forecast frequency, our model introduces predictions specifically engineered for renewable energy production. The model forecasts 100-meter wind speeds (roughly at turbine-height) for precise wind-energy output, alongside high-resolution cloud cover and sun radiation levels to help solar farms estimate how much light they will receive on the ground.”

In terms of consumer-facing benefits, WeatherNext 3 is rolling out to Google Search, Maps, and the Gemini app. Google says to expect “dramatically improve[d] longer term forecasts.”

When planning a day or more ahead, people will see up to 50% more accurate precipitation forecasts — with the greatest improvements in regions where forecasts have historically been less reliable.

title: Authors push back as publishers and agents make claims on Anthropic settlement
snippet: Authors say publishers seem to be claiming more than their fair share of settlement payments.
fullText:
Some authors hoping to receive their share of Anthropic’s $1.5 billion copyright settlement said they received surprising emails this week — emails informing them that someone else was making a claim on their payments.

Anthropic settled a copyright class action suit last year, after a judge ruled that training AI models on copyrighted material is legal under fair use doctrine, but pirating that material was not. The deal received final approval in July, allowing the payments to move forward.

Under the terms of the settlement, the authors of nearly 500,000 titles will be paid $3,000 for each pirated work. If the book is still in-print with a traditional publisher, the money will be split 50-50 between author and publisher. If the book was self-published, or if the publisher reverted the rights by allowing the book to go out-of-print, then the author should get the entire payment.

But writers have been posting on social media that publishers seem to be claiming more than their fair share of some payments. For example, mystery and thriller author April Henry asked, “WTF is HarperCollins playing at? They claimed one of my books on the Anthropic Settlement that reverted back at least 17 years ago AND on the same day I got a credit alert saying they had been added as my employer! (which they never were).”

At the popular blog Writers Beware, Victoria Strauss wrote that she’s been receiving author complaints that fall into two broad categories: one where publishers are seeking payment for works that they no longer have a legitimate claim on (because the rights have reverted), and another where publishers are seeking a full 100% payment when they’re only entitled to 50%.

In both cases, Strauss said she’s “reluctant to attribute to malice what can be plausibly explained by poor recordkeeping” — and she noted that some publishers have already said this is a mistake that they’ve asked Anthropic to fix.

Similarly, Authors Guild CEO Mary Rasenberger told The New York Times that she doesn’t see this as “a grab by the publishers” and that she doesn’t believe publishers are “specifically trying to screw any author over.” Instead, she argued that this is the predictable result of bad record-keeping and a confusing settlement process.

Strauss also acknowledged that any complaints she’s seen are just “a peek through a small crack in a massive wall.”

“But the unusually large number of reports I’ve received over the last two days, as well as the fact that authors are reporting the exact same errors over and over, suggest to me that these aren’t the kind of routine glitches you might expect from such a large operation, but something much more wide[s]pread and systemic,” she wrote.

And publishers aren’t the only ones seeking a cut of the payments. Strauss said she’s gotten complaints that a number of literary agencies are also making claims, which she said is surprising since “agents are not rightsholders in the books that they sell.”

Author Courtney Milan (the pen name of former law clerk and law professor Heidi Bond) was more blunt in a post on Bluesky, writing, “Apparently some agents are trying to claim percentages on the Anthropic settlement, and I do not REMOTELY think they should do this, what the fuck, stop that shit!”

Milan and the Authors Guild also shared more details about how authors can dispute their payment allocations. (One tricky issue: When the rights to a specific book reverted. In order for an author to make a 100% claim on a book, the rights reversion needs to have happened before August 10, 2022, which is the “download date” in the settlement.)

title: Belkin says its new ‘BoostSolid’ Qi2 batteries last 3x longer than your other magnetic power banks
snippet: During IFA 2026, Belkin announced a new lineup of magnetic Qi2 battery banks using a new solid-state technology. The two UltraCharge Pro models can charge devices at up to 15W wirelessly, but they have more tricks in the sleeve. more…
fullText:
During IFA 2026, Belkin announced a new lineup of magnetic Qi2 battery banks using a new solid-state technology. The two UltraCharge Pro models can charge devices at up to 15W wirelessly, but they have more tricks in the sleeve.

It’s a little difficult to find good magnetic batteries that offer a reliable experience. The Qi2 standard isn’t exactly new, but plenty of batteries that snap to the back of your phone might not be capable of reaching 15W.

Belkin announced two new magnetic Qi2 batteries. They follow a common split into a 5,000mAh and a 10,000mAh power bank. Belkin says both UltraCharge Pro batteries are built on what it’s calling “BoostSolid” technology using internal gel layers for better performance, which it’s advertising lasts up to three times longer than other power banks.

That estimate comes from its ability to retain 80% capacity after 1,000 charge cycles. That’s a five-year lifespan on a full charge cycle every two days.

	

UltraCharge Pro Slim 5K
UltraCharge Pro 10K

The UltraCharge Pro Slim battery is the most pocket-friendly. It takes up little extra bulk compared to the larger model, but it only provides 5,000mAh of power. The thicker version has twice the capacity and adds a display for real-time battery status and alerts.

Both are certified for Qi2 15W wireless charging, but the UltraCharge Pro 10K is able to reach 60W wired charging from a single port, which opens it up to charge larger devices.

If you need something that will charge a laptop or gaming handhelds, the 10,000mAh UltraCharge Pro is likely the better bet. The Slim version is just as useful if space is a heavy consideration.

Belkin’s UltraCharge Pro Slim 5K and UltraCharge Pro 10K Qi2 batteries will be available starting this month from retailers like Amazon and Belkin’s website.

title: OpenAI confirms ‘wiki incident,’ says it’s ‘working on a framework’ for more disclosure
snippet: OpenAI acknowledged its role in a recently reported incident where AI agents took over a German wiki forum.
fullText:
OpenAI has acknowledged its role in a recently reported incident where AI agents took over a German wiki forum. The company also said it’s “past time” to “define standards” around how it shares information around incidents where its technology behaves in unexpected ways.

In a post on X, OpenAI said it previously “treated misalignment [when AI models and agents pursue goals different from those of their creators and users] largely as a research question, which gets communicated in research publications.” But as misalignment has “caused new types of real-world impact,” the company said its approach needs “to expand for this new phase of model capabilities.”

On Friday, Reuters reported that OpenAI agents had escaped from their testing environment and “hijacked” an obscure German wiki forum, turning it into a message board for other agents. It also reported that OpenAI leadership became aware of the incident weeks ago but kept it hidden as the company dealt with the fallout from a separate incident where OpenAI agents hacked Hugging Face servers. (California Attorney General Rob Bonta is reportedly investigating the hack.)

A company spokesperson told Reuters that OpenAI could not “meaningfully respond to claims or findings on a report that we have not had an opportunity to review,” but they insisted that the company’s legal team had not discouraged an investigation.

In its more recent social media post, OpenAI said it had considered the “wiki incident” to be “an instance of misalignment similar” to others that it had already shared. The company contrasted this with “the Hugging Face incident,” where it “followed a traditional security incident response playbook.”

During a media briefing this week, Jacob Steinhardt, founder and CEO of nonprofit research lab Transluce, told reporters that the tools being developed and tested by AI labs are “fundamentally difficult to control and have significant risk of leaking out of the lab.” So Steinhardt argued, “We need to hold this technology to at least the same standards we hold other high-risk scientific research to.”

OpenAI’s statement also gestured at the need for more standards, stating that both OpenAI and “the larger AI community do not yet have a clear standard for how to report misalignment that shows up during training, evaluation, and deployment, including examples that don’t look like traditional security incidents but could provide insight into AI behavior and future risks.”

In the absence of that standard, OpenAI said it’s “working on a framework and will share it in upcoming weeks, and in parallel we’re working with dozens of government regulatory agencies worldwide on these issues.”

OpenAI isn’t the only AI company dealing with these issues, as both Meta and Anthropic have acknowledged incidents where their agents misbehaved.

title: Govee’s new ceiling light and LED strips are mood boosters with some AI sprinkled in
snippet: Govee launched a handful of new lighting options at IFA 2026, ranging from another ceiling light that responds to daylight to COB LED strips that use prompts to generate your lighting conditions. more…
fullText:
Govee launched a handful of new lighting options at IFA 2026, ranging from another ceiling light that responds to daylight to COB LED strips that use prompts to generate your lighting conditions.

Govee has been pushing to become one of the biggest names in smart home lighting, competing with massive brands like Philips Hue, GE Cync, and more. It’s recently begun expanding into ceiling lights, with a release earlier in the year that hinged on creating “living art.”

The ceiling light collection is growing with Govee’s IFA releases. The new Govee Sky Ceiling Light is an “AI-powered mood-responsive” option, because this is 2026 and every device needs a little AI. Right?

Calling it an AI light does it a bit of a disservice, because it sounds like a genuinely cool concept. Govee is working around the comfort wavelengths using the “vitality spectrum technology.” In essence, the ceiling light produces wavelengths that make up for deficiencies in natural lighting. Govee says this helps users maintain alertness during darker days.

	

The Sky Ceiling Light has a color temperature range from 1,000K to 10,000K, reaching up to 7,000 lumens of white light. Users will get the most out of it by using the “DaySync” feature in the Govee app, which uses weather and time data to adjust comfortable lighting conditions.

The massive ceiling light comes at a cost of $399.

On the more vibrant side of things, the Govee COB Strip Light 2 Pro uses AI in a similar way. Users can write prompts to generate lighting conditions for their space. It’s all need-dependent, and the AI Lighting Bot 2.0 model will create light sequences for different scenarios.

COB lights produce flicker-free output, and the Strip Light 2 Pro has 1,344 LEDs per meter with a triple-layer groove design. Govee says this ensures flawless output in single-color and dynamic color modes. The color temperature range echoes that of the ceiling light at 1,000K to 10,000K, and it uses Govee’s LumiBlend+ color engine to produce accurate colors.

The Pro model is Govee’s flagship LED strip at $169 per 5m, but the COB Strip Light 2 will also be available at a more affordable $99.

Govee’s Sky Ceiling Light and Strip Light 2 Pro will be available starting today from it’s website and at retailers like Amazon.

title: TCL’s first NXTPAPER phone with AMOLED is also one of its most flagship-like, coming to US
snippet: After showing off a proof-of-concept back at CES 2026 earlier this year, TCL is officially making its first NXTPAPER phones with AMOLED displays – the TCL P80 series. more…
fullText:
After showing off a proof-of-concept back at CES 2026 earlier this year, TCL is officially making its first NXTPAPER phones with AMOLED displays – the TCL P80 series.

TCL’s NXTPAPER display tech is more than just a matte coating, but the one part that takes the whole thing down a notch has been the panel technology. While NXTPAPER displays typically look good, they lack the vibrance and brightness of the AMOLED (or OLED) panels used on most other modern smartphones. That’s finally changing, with the first new releases dropping this week.

TCL P80, P80 Pro, and P80 Ultra offer up a 1.5K NXTPAPER AMOLED display and some of the highest-end packages TCL has put together so far – though still not quite in flagship territory. All three phones are based on MediaTek chips, with Ultra and Pro using Dimensity 7400 Elite and the base model a Dimensity 7300 Elite. These are upper-mid-range chips that are still a whole lot more powerful than what TCL’s phones usually bring to the table. They’ve all got a 6.83-inch display.

The TCL P80 Ultra has two 50MP cameras on the back including a telephoto lens, up to 512GB of storage, 8GB of RAM, a 6,800 mAh battery, and IP68 dust/water resistance.  TCL P80 Pro is virtually identical, but the second 50MP camera is now an 8MP ultrawide. The base TCL P80 also has a 50MP main camera and 8MP ultrawide, but has the aforementioned drop in chipset, as well as limiting itself to 256GB of storage at most, while still offering 8GB of RAM. It also drops down to a 6,000 mAh battery. 

	

These phones launch in Europe starting today at €349, €429, and €549, respectively.

TCL says these phones will come to the US eventually, but there’s no exact word on when. TCL is supporting the Ultra with 7 years of OS and security updates, while the Pro and base models drop to 3 years of OS updates, but stick with 7 years of security updates.

title: Krafton doubles down on India with another $250M bet beyond gaming
snippet: Krafton's planned investment in India is set to surpass $500 million with its latest commitment.
fullText:
Krafton, the South Korean gaming company behind titles including PUBG and Battlegrounds Mobile India (BGMI), plans to invest another $250 million in India over the next three to four years as it pushes beyond gaming into AI, robotics, and deep tech.

Announced Friday, the new commitment will take Krafton’s total planned investment in India to more than $500 million, including the over $250 million it had already invested in the country since 2021. The funds also come in addition to Krafton’s commitment to a $670 million India-focused growth fund it unveiled with South Korean internet conglomerate Naver and investor Mirae Asset in December 2025. At the time, Krafton said it would contribute around $137 million at the fund’s first close. The new $250 million pledge is separate from the growth fund, the company confirmed to TechCrunch.

India has become a key market for Krafton, giving the gaming publisher access to the world’s most populous country, with more than a billion internet subscribers and over 700 million smartphone users. Krafton initially built its India business around gaming, led by BGMI, a revamped and localized version of PUBG that has surpassed 260 million downloads. In recent years, the company has also used investments in Indian startups to broaden its business beyond games.

Krafton’s run in India has not always been smooth. The Indian government banned PUBG Mobile in 2020, along with hundreds of Chinese-linked apps, as tensions between New Delhi and Beijing escalated. Krafton stepped in after that and introduced BGMI in 2021. The company dropped Tencent Games as the game’s publisher in India and moved its India servers to Microsoft’s Azure cloud, changes that came as Krafton worked to address New Delhi’s concerns.

However, in 2022, BGMI was itself banned in India, before the federal government allowed it to return on a three-month trial basis the following year. Krafton has continued to build around the franchise since its return and plans to launch BGMI Lite in India by the end of 2026.

Despite the early setbacks, Krafton continued to invest in India and has so far backed about 18 companies, including four to five gaming studios, the company confirmed to TechCrunch. Its investments include Nodwin Gaming, Loco, Pratilipi, Kuku FM, and One Impression, among others.

The new investment commitment comes after Krafton chairman Chang Byung-gyu met Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi earlier on Friday. The two discussed opportunities for India and South Korea to work more closely across gaming, technology, and other emerging sectors, Krafton said.

Krafton has also been building out its local operations. Last year, it acquired Pune-based Nautilus Mobile, the studio behind the Real Cricket franchise. The company also recently launched KIGI Academy, an industry-academia program aimed at training talent in game development and digital creation.

title: Google Pics is Workspace’s new ‘pro-level’ AI image creator & editor
snippet: Following the announcement at I/O 2026 in May, Google Pics is launching in general availability today. more…
fullText:
Following the announcement at I/O 2026 in May, Google Pics is launching in general availability today.

Google Pics, which comes after Google Vids, is “built natively into Google Workspace.” You can click on an image in Google Docs or Slides and access the Pics editor as an overlay to start editing. An update in the coming weeks will let you edit images uploaded to Google Drive.

You can also access the tool from pics.new:

Besides generating a new image (with multiple options offered), you can import files from your computer, Google Drive, or Google Photos to start editing.

	

Leveraging Nano Banana, Google Pics offers “precise, object-based image editing.” Tools let you: 

Select and edit individual objects within an image 

Edit, reformat, or even translate individual text elements 

Crop your image for web, social media, print, or digital

Upscale your image to 2K or 4K

Process multiple edits at once, and revert any unwanted changes easily

The object segmentation capability lets you isolate a specific part and leave other parts of the image untouched. After selecting, you just provide text comments with the ability to “execute multiple edits at once.” Similarly, you can edit text that appears in images without changing anything else, which also allows for translation. 

Pics eliminates the frustration of wrangling pixels and feeling like you need to be a graphic designer to deliver a great image.

Based on the same editor as other Workspace apps, you can invite others to collaborate and share images via a link. Enterprise use cases include:

Create and translate social, digital, and web assets for global markets

Bring product concepts to life by placing them into any background or context

Brainstorm print designs, event collateral, or branded merchandise

Develop flyers, business cards, and much more

Google Pics is available for the following tiers starting today:

Google AI Pro and Ultra personal plans

Workspace Business Standard, Business Plus, Enterprise Standard, and Enterprise Plus plans

title: Poco F9 Pro and F9 Ultra launch with 185Hz panels, 8 Elite Gen 5 chips, and huge batteries
snippet: Xiaomi sub-brand Poco is officially expanding its flagship smartphone line with the launch of the Poco F9 Pro and Poco F9 Ultra. more…
fullText:
Xiaomi sub-brand Poco is officially expanding its flagship smartphone line with the launch of the Poco F9 Pro and Poco F9 Ultra.

Under the hood, the top-tier Poco F9 Ultra packs Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 processor paired with up to 16GB of RAM and 1TB of UFS 4.1 storage. The standard Poco F9 Pro relies on the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 V Series (SM8850-1-AB) with up to 12GB of RAM and 512GB of storage. Both handsets incorporate a dedicated 12nm VisionBoost D8 graphics chip to handle AI frame insertion and super-resolution processing.

On the front, both devices feature HyperRGB AMOLED panels with a 185Hz refresh rate and peak brightness up to 4,500 nits. The Poco F9 Pro features a 6.59-inch display with a 2510 x 1156 resolution, while the Poco F9 Ultra expands to a 6.9-inch display with a 2608 x 1200 resolution. Both screens feature 480Hz 10-point touch sampling, 4800Hz instant touch sampling, Gorilla Glass 7i protection, and integrated ultrasonic fingerprint sensors.

Camera hardware sees a major overhaul on both models, starting with a shared 200MP primary sensor with optical image stabilization (OIS) and 4K video recording. The secondary camera configurations branch off from there. 

	

The Poco F9 Pro pairs the main camera with a 50MP floating telephoto lens capable of 2.5x optical zoom and an 8MP ultra-wide sensor. The Poco F9 Ultra steps up to a 50MP periscope telephoto lens with 5x optical zoom alongside a 50MP ultra-wide sensor. Both phones include a 32MP front-facing selfie camera.

Audio performance has been tuned in partnership with Bose. The F9 Pro comes equipped with symmetrical dual stereo speakers, whereas the Poco F9 Ultra introduces a 2.1-channel audio configuration that combines dual stereo speakers with an independent 1620 rear subwoofer.

Power endurance is handled by a 6,330mAh battery on the F9 Pro, while the F9 Ultra houses a, frankly, massive 8,050mAh silicon-carbon battery with a 16% silicon content ratio. Both models share the same charging speeds: 100W wired fast charging, 50W wireless charging, 27W wired reverse charging, and 22.5W wireless reverse charging.

Additional standard hardware specifications include IP68 dust and water resistance, NFC support, and Xiaomi HyperOS 3 running out of the box. Color choices for the F9 Pro include Black, White, and Aurora Green, which features a glow-in-the-dark rear cover. The F9 Ultra is available in Black and Dark Cherry with a glass fiber finish and interactive lighting accents on the rear housing.

Pricing for the Poco F9 Pro starts at $699 for the 12GB/256GB base model (early-bird $649) and reaches $769 for the 12GB/512GB tier (early-bird $699). The Poco F9 Ultra starts at $799 for the 12GB/256GB option (early bird $729), $949 for the 16GB/512GB option (early bird $799), and tops out at $1,199 for the 16GB/1TB option (early bird $1,059). Global availability and localized ordering options are available directly on the official Poco Global page and Xiaomi launch portal.

title: How do Apple Refurbished products compare with Amazon and Walmart?
snippet: If you’re willing to exercise a little patience rather than rushing out to buy a shiny new Apple product on launch day, then Apple’s refurbished store has always been an excellent option. Typically, there will be around a three-month wait between a product launch and the first refurbished models appearing on Apple’s website. Other companies offers their own alternatives, like Amazon Renewed and Walmart Restored, but it’s important to understand the different standards and warranties that apply … more…
fullText:
If you’re willing to exercise a little patience rather than rushing out to buy a shiny new Apple product on launch day, then Apple’s refurbished store has always been an excellent option. Typically, there will be around a three-month wait between a product launch and the first refurbished models appearing on Apple’s website.

Other companies offers their own alternatives, like Amazon Renewed and Walmart Restored, but it’s important to understand the different standards and warranties that apply …

Apple Certified Refurbished

Buying from Apple’s Certified Refurbished store gets you a typical discount of 15% on a product that will be indistinguishable from new. Specifically, Apple guarantees all of the following:

Full inspection and testing by Apple

A brand new outer shell, so there will never be any marks or scratches

A brand new battery, so you’ll get the same battery life as usual

All original accessories and cables are included

Apple’s standard one-year warranty applies in exactly the same way as a new product

The same eligibility for AppleCare+

Literally the only difference you’ll see is that products are supplied in a plain white box rather than the original packaging.

Amazon Renewed

Amazon Renewed can offer more competitive pricing, but it’s worth being aware that you’re not getting the same guarantees as to condition:

Inspection and testing by the seller, not by Apple

Used outer shell, so expect marks and scratches (see below)

Used battery, only guaranteed to exceed 80% of the original capacity

Accessories may not be genuine Apple ones

90-day Amazon warranty, instead of 1-year Apple one

As for marks and scratches, Amazon offers three tier quality tiers:

Premium/Excellent: No signs of cosmetic damage when held 12 inches away

Good: Light scratches, barely visible when holding the device 12 inches away

Acceptable: Scratches that are easily seen and felt

Walmart Restored

Walmart Restored is a lot vaguer than Amazon on what you’re getting for your money:

Inspection and testing by the seller, not by Apple

No promises as to cosmetic condition, only “like-new performance and reliability”

No specifics on the battery condition beyond the above

No information on accessories

Seller warranty, instead of 1-year Apple one

The seller warranty is for one year on the Restored Premium tier, and 90 days on Like New, Good, and Fair tiers. The company isn’t specific about its definitions for each tier.

9to5Mac’s Take

If you want a product indistinguishable from new in terms of both condition and Apple warranty, then it’s clear that Apple’s refurbished store is the place to go.

Amazon Renewed can, however, offer significantly better pricing, so if you’re willing to accept the compromises listed above, you may consider this a decent deal. In particular, if you’re opting to take our advice to save money by upgrading to the iPhone 17 Pro instead of this year’s model (when the only accessory you’re sacrificing is the cable), there are some attractive deals here:

512GB iPhone 17 Pro Deep Blue $1,170 (Reg. $1,299 new) – all-time low

512GB iPhone 17 Pro Silver $1,171 (Reg. $1,299 new) – within $1 of all-time low

As for Walmart Restored, I’d worry about the extreme vagueness of the promises, but you do have the option of returning them if you aren’t happy.

by  Terrence O'Brien

Sep 6, 2026, 7:04 PM UTC

Image: Isar Aerospace

Terrence O'Brien

 

is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

German company Isar Aerospace has successfully launched Europe’s first entirely commercial orbital rocket. It attempted to achieve the feat last March, but that lasted all of 30 seconds before the vehicle crashed into the sea and exploded. This time the company managed to get the two-stage Spectrum into low Earth orbit from a Norwegian spaceport.

CEO and Co-Founder Daniel Metzler said in a press release:

“Today, Isar Aerospace opened space from Continental Europe. Launch continues to be the largest bottleneck for the global space industry and from today on, there is a true alternative for commercial and institutional customers … Europe now has sovereign access to space. We have entered into a new chapter for European spaceflight.”

Until now, Europe has been largely reliant on Arianespace and Avio, which are largely funded by governments. The current global political climate makes the accomplishment particularly important for European countries that might view the United States as a less reliable partner at the moment and that have been cut off from Russian Soyuz rockets by the country’s invasion of Ukraine. The European Space Agency has also made “buy European” a cornerstone of its policies.

title: Is iKairos a Robot, or Jewelry? It’s Both, and It Wants to Be Your Ever-Present AI Memory Keeper
snippet: This wearable-cum-desktop robot is one of the most unique AI devices I saw at IFA in Berlin.
fullText:
If I said the words “wearable robot” to you, you might initially feel confused, but when you see iKairos in person, the idea quickly makes sense.

iKairos is effectively a modular system with a circular AI device at its heart, about the size of a large smartwatch face. The device, called the “neural core,” can either be worn around your neck as a pendant or slotted into a cute desktop robot to form the head.

I met iKairos, the creation of Singaporean startup Lingverse, at IFA in Berlin. There are a huge number of small AI devices at the show, but this one caught my eye for its flexibility and modularity. It falls into two different product categories at once — wearables and robots — making it a unique proposition. At least these will be the two options at launch. Lingverse has plans to expand the range of hardware options over time.

Most standalone AI devices are designed for specific uses, such as note-taking, life-logging or productivity. Of these, iKairos occupies a spot somewhere between life-logging and productivity. It ambiently keeps tabs on your conversations, your environment and your preferences, both to preserve your memories and make suggestions that can be helpful in your daily life.

iKairos can also take the form of a desktop robot.

The ability to switch out the devices that play host to the neural core means the iKairos device can capture multiple perspectives in different settings. I could understand the way you work at home, for example, along with where you like to go in your spare time, who the important people are in your life and what you do to relax.

This central module has a display, with a pair of cartoon eyes, but it also slides open to reveal a camera that can be used to capture photos or video. I like the fact that the camera isn’t always out and always on. It gives you, and those around you, a level of privacy that AI peripherals with cameras front and center simply don’t offer. In addition to this physical shutter, there’s also a light underneath the camera that makes it obvious when it’s switched on.

Voice detection and capture are local to the device, and any data processed in the cloud is encrypted, according to Lingverse. The company also stresses that user data is not used for training purposes.

The main idea behind Kairos is that it captures the context needed to understand who you are and how you live, but I’m still a little fuzzy on what it actually does with information. It can identify insights and patterns, as well as take snapshots of your memories, which you can ask it to recall for you later, but it’s not clear exactly what its killer function is right now.

In robot mode, iKairos is pretty cute.

I’ll be interested to see, when the device finally hits the market, whether that context can then be used in conjunction with agentic AI applications, which can proactively take actions on your behalf. I could imagine it sending an apology message and rescheduling a meeting if you were running late, for example, or reminding you that you said you would drop into the store to pick something up as you drive past.

Lingverse is still building iKairos, so there’s no pricing or availability details to share right now, but if you’re interested in early access, you can join the waitlist on the iKairos website.

title: Reports describe two ways for Apple to make more money; only one is good
snippet: There were two reports in the last few days indicating different routes for Apple to make more money by boosting Services revenue. In my view, it should absolutely do the first of these, but not the second – and it appears Phil Schiller may agree … more…
fullText:
There were two reports in the last few days indicating different routes for Apple to make more money by boosting Services revenue. 

In my view, it should absolutely do the first of these, but not the second – and it appears Phil Schiller may agree …

Let’s start by summarizing the two reports.

Home security & monitoring service

On Friday, Bloomberg suggested that Apple may be planning a new home security and monitoring service to sit alongside some of the new home hardware we’re expecting.

Apple is planning a privacy-centric home security camera and automation device that will use AI to monitor the surrounding environment instead of actual video footage. It will tap into a new home security and monitoring service.

Squeezing more revenue from the App Store

A second report from the same source on Sunday said that the company is looking at ways to squeeze more revenue and profit from the App Store.

Ternus and services chief Eddy Cue want to make even more money from the App Store and figure out ways to raise margins and squeeze additional recurring revenue from the platform.

Apple should not take the latter approach

Tackling these in reverse order, I think the second approach would be a very big mistake. 

Apple’s effective monopoly on the sale of iPhone apps has come under fire from regulators around the world. In most countries, if you want to sell an iPhone app, you are forced to do so through the official App Store, and that leaves you with no choice but to accept the company’s terms on a take-it-or-leave-it basis.

I understand a common view is that nobody forces anyone to buy an iPhone or make apps for it, but that is not the reality of how even the most laissez-faire forms of capitalism work: even the US has had antitrust legislation in place since 1890. When you achieve a certain level of market dominance, then constraints are imposed on how you need to behave in order to ensure you don’t abuse your position.

Trying to squeeze even more money from the App Store is very much the antithesis of skating to where the puck is headed, and Phil Schiller reportedly shares this view as Bloomberg suggests it’s one of the reasons he’s stepped down now.

Schiller, on the other hand, seems to believe that such moves will only further irk developers and governments. While there was no internal blowup or anything like that, it’s something he wanted no part of.

Innovative services are the way to go

Introducing new innovative services that people will want to buy, in contrast, is absolutely the right thing for Apple to do. I can easily see value in the company offering a home security monitoring service.

I argued back in 2024 that making its own smart home camera would be one of the … smartest things the company could do. I said the same again about rumours of an Apple smart doorbell. Adding an optional Services component to security products makes perfect sense for two reasons.

First, there are all the privacy arguments I’ve made before. HomeKit Secure Video has already made a major contribution to ensuring the privacy of security camera feeds. If there is one company I’d trust to perform AI analysis of security camera footage, it’s Apple.

Second, Apple is of course best placed to fully integrate security hardware and services within a HomeKit environment. I’m sure there will be many other areas where Apple can offer similar benefits.

To me, the key is that Apple needs to adopt the same approach to services it does to hardware. Make great products that lead to people willingly parting with their money and doing so with a smile on their face. Not squeezing money in a way that irritates customers, developers, and regulators alike.

What’s your take on this? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

title: Google Home update fixes alarms, improves media & smart home voice controls
snippet: The latest Google Home update is fixing issues with alarms that some users were experiencing while also improving media and smart home voice controls in Google’s continued effort to address pain points in Gemini for Home. more…
fullText:
The latest Google Home update is fixing issues with alarms that some users were experiencing while also improving media and smart home voice controls in Google’s continued effort to address pain points in Gemini for Home.

The most noticeable upgrade in the latest Google Home update should be around voice commands. On smart speakers and displays, Gemini “now understands a broader range” of commands regarding media and smart home devices. You can also chain commands in the same sentence. 

Google explains:

Expanded capabilities and understanding for media controls: Gemini on speakers and displays now understands a broader range of voice commands across media and home device controls. And, you can now combine media commands with other commands to get things done faster.

Try saying:

“Turn off the lights and stop the music.”

“Skip this song and turn on the backyard lights.”

“Stop captions on this video.”

This update should also fix an issue with Google Keep integration as well as an issue that was preventing users from creating or editing alarms and lists. Seeing as smart speakers and display are very often used as an alarm clock, that’s welcome news.

	

Rounding out this update, the Google Home app should clean up any rogue automations from third-party apps. The automations editor should also be a lot easier to use now, as starters, conditions, and actions are now listed in alphabetical order automatically. 

More on Google Home:

Google Home update restores support for older Chromecast streamers, Home Mini

Google Home update lets you set light color temperature to your favorite kelvin using voice commands

Google Home update adds support for viewing third-party cameras from Wyze, Eufy, more

title: Roku launches its first OLED TVs, available now starting at $999
snippet: Roku is expanding its first-party TV lineup with new OLED models that start at $999. more…
fullText:
Roku is expanding its first-party TV lineup with new OLED models that start at $999.

The new Roku Pro Series OLED TV and Roku Pro Series LX OLED TV are just what the names imply – first-party television sets from Roku that use OLED panels. That means getting deeper blacks and more vibrant colors, while also seeing benefits like wider viewing angles.

Roku explains:

Ultra-wide viewing angles give everyone a great sight line, while OLED technology delivers vibrant color and blacks that are truly black. From shadowy thrillers to bright animated favorites, scenes feel deeper, richer, and more immersive. To make it even better, there’s no need to worry about adjusting picture settings before pressing play. Roku Smart Picture Max automatically tunes the TV to suit what you’re watching, so every show, movie, game, and live event is optimized without any extra work from you.

The company also touts “an ultra-thin profile and slim metal bezel” for the hardware, as well as built-in cable management on the back of the TV. There’s also an “Automatic Game Mode” for consoles to improve input lag and other factors, which should pair nicely with the 144Hz refresh rate. The included remote has backlit buttons, customizable shortcuts, and a Bluetooth headphone mode, as well as a remote finder feature.

	

The base Roku Pro Series OLED TV starts at $999 for a 55-inch model, while a 65-inch model is also available. Both can be purchased starting today only on Amazon. The LX models, meanwhile, are coming in October from $1,299.

title: AI compute provider Nscale is looking for $3.5B in pre-IPO financing
snippet: Nscale, which recently struck a $45 billion deal with Anthropic, is in talks to raise additional funds in anticipation of an upcoming IPO.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

2:12 PM PDT · September 4, 2026

Image Credits:David Paul Morris/Bloomberg / Getty Images

		

							

											
									

					

	

Nscale, a British AI infrastructure company founded just two years ago, has said it may go public as early as later this month. Ahead of that expected IPO, the company is reportedly in talks to raise an additional $3.5 billion.

Bloomberg reported Friday that the company is looking to sell $1.5 billion in convertible notes — a type of loan that can later convert into company stock — to a group of investors, while also seeking an additional $2 billion in financing from Nvidia.

Nvidia also participated in the firm’s Series B funding round in March, a $1.1 billion raise led by investment fund Aker. Nscale hailed its round as “the largest Series B in European history.” The company’s Series A round, in December of 2024, raised $155 million.

TechCrunch reached out to Nscale and Nvidia for comment. 

AI infrastructure startups have seen immense growth amid the current era of AI enthusiasm, wherein compute has become a competitive currency.

Nscale recently signed a large deal with Anthropic worth approximately $45 billion. Earlier this week, reports emerged that Nscale had been telling potential investors that it has approximately $103 billion in revenue following the deal. That figure isn’t current sales; it’s a projection based on signed customer leases, according to The Information.
