fullText:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on e-bikes, power stations, and how to work anywhere, follow Thomas Ricker. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

How it started

With a deep breath, I took the cable seething with 800W of solar power and plugged it directly into a standard wall jack in my home. Nothing sparked, nothing smoked, and by the end of that sunny summer day, my electricity bill had dropped to nearly $0.

As unnerving as it sounds to treat a common household power outlet like a power input, these DIY plug-in solar kits, sometimes called balcony solar, have proven to be safe and effective for years already in Europe, and are slowly making their way into the US to democratize the production of energy. They transform solar from a high-barrier capital improvement (starting at around $15,000) requiring contractors, engineering permits, and utility preapproval, into an consumer appliance you can buy at a supermarket (starting around $300) and hang from a balcony railing or prop against a wall — all without the help of an electrician.

Traditional plug-in solar kits include a few solar panels and a small microinverter that ties itself to the electrical grid. The microinverter converts solar energy into power that’s prioritized for use by devices inside your home.

Optionally, you can add a battery to the kit to store any surplus energy produced during the day. That way, you can continue to cut your costs by feeding that stored energy back into the home when the sun goes down. These so-called power stations can also be used to power a fridge and other critical devices during a blackout. They start at around $500 for a small 1kWh battery or $1,500 for 3kWh.

I live in Europe, where millions of households, including as estimated 1.5M in Germany, have purchased plug-in solar systems over the last few years to gain a modicum of energy independence. They’re so popular, even Ikea sells them (though they’re actually just EcoFlow resellers).

Plug-in solar’s popularity has been fueled by two things. Oil and gas prices have surged ever since Russia invaded Ukraine, and have remained high amid the ongoing US war with Iran. Meanwhile, global prices for solar panels and batteries have fallen to record lows — though US consumers face higher costs due to Trump’s tariffs on panels and batteries and the elimination of solar tax credits. Nevertheless, plug-in solar is finally getting a foothold in those amber waves of grain.

Historically, utility regulations in the US treated a budget solar panel in a garden like a massive 10kW rooftop array. Now, over a dozen states have passed laws or introduced bills to legalize the deployment of plug-in solar systems. The rules vary, but in general they allow for qualifying plug-in solar systems to be installed without utility preapproval so long as they meet safety requirements, prevent individual circuits from overloading, and shut down during a power outage to keep line workers safe.

How it’s going

I’ve had a modest 400W plug-in system operating on my rooftop deck in the Netherlands. In those 21 months of use, it produced 709kWh, saving me about €225 (about $260) — enough to nearly offset the purchase price of my kit. It will take longer to offset the rather large $1,800 power station it all plugs into when I’m home. But as an avid vanlifer, I get a ton of extra value out of that emergency battery, which also enables me to live and work off grid for months at a time.

People operating a plug-in solar system in sunnier climates with maxed out solar arrays will recoup costs much faster. European plug-in solar systems can feed as much as 800W into the home, while US states typically support up to 1200W. And kits often support even greater solar capacity so long as it’s diverted to a battery.

In the US, plug-in solar is now legal in Virginia, Maine, Colorado, Maryland, New Jersey, Connecticut, Vermont, and New Hampshire, ever since Utah pioneered the state-level reclassification of plug-in solar as a small household appliance last year. Legislation is awaiting governor signature in California and New York, while another half-dozen states have introduced bills.

In Europe, of the 27 EU member states, only Sweden and Hungary still prohibit plug-in solar devices.

What happens next

European adoption of plug-in solar systems will almost certainly continue its upward trend so long as solar and battery prices keep falling — it’s not like the geopolitical situation will bring energy prices down anytime soon. US adoption could be in for a hockey stick moment of growth just as soon as California — the state with the highest residential electricity rates — signs plug-in solar into law.

Now that the legal dominos have started falling in the US, the nascent plug-in solar category has piqued the interest of companies focused on home energy. EcoFlow, Bluetti, Anker, and many others, are all trying to capitalize on the surge of interest, giving renters and budget-conscious consumers a wider selection of kits to choose from.

Already in the last few months, we’ve seen EcoFlow launch its more capable Stream 2 series alongside Bluetti’s Balco series. Both of these plug-in solar systems are built on modular architectures so that owners can expand from entry-level solar generation to a larger, whole home energy system over time.

I can attest that plug-in solar is a slippery slope. First you buy the microinverter and a few solar panels, then more panels and a battery to store the energy surplus, and then you start looking at how you can extract even more energy out of thin air. Because once you start looking closely at the power you’re paying for, canceling it out with “free energy” becomes an addictive game.

Plug-in solar isn’t going to replace utility-scale solar farms or 10kW rooftop arrays, but it fills the missing bottom layer of the clean energy transition. My two-year-old kit has already nearly paid for itself. Beyond the savings, I like that I’m reducing my contribution to climate change, and that feeling’s invaluable.

And who knows, maybe a new US administration will arrive in a few years to give the entire sector a goose, instead of actively working against solar and handing the future of energy production to China, uncontested.

By the Way

Plug-in solar systems just became legal across Great Britain on August 27th. Retailers like Lidl, B&Q, Argos, Currys, and Amazon are selling solar-only kits in stores and online. It took the unusual step of forbidding battery-integrated systems, but they’re being explored for future inclusion.

New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill signed the Garden State Balcony Solar Act into law earlier this week, legalizing setups up to 1,200W on 120V outlets. But the law takes effect on March 1st, 2027.

Read this

This New York Times piece takes a sober look at the transformative effects plug-in solar could have on American energy production and consumption.

title: MapQuest is back, at the top of the charts, and rushing to add Android Auto support
snippet: In a “that’s a name I’ve not heard in a long time” move, MapQuest is back to being a household name, as the original mapping app has found itself as the top of app store charts – it’s also rushing to add support for Android Auto. more…
fullText:
In a “that’s a name I’ve not heard in a long time” move, MapQuest is back to being a household name, as the original mapping app has found itself as the top of app store charts – it’s also rushing to add support for Android Auto.

MapQuest has been around for 30 years, but it only entered the modern era back in 2024 when it relaunched with a private mobile mapping app with a pitch around being “anti-Big Tech.” That app has since shut down, and a full MapQuest app arrived earlier this year.

Now, that app is at the top of app store charts.

On iOS, MapQuest is the #8 free app on the App Store (as of Aug 30), and #5 on Android’s Play Store (as of today) – at least in the US. In a press release, MapQuest says this is “the highest chart position in the brand’s 30-year history” and that usage is “roughly 50 times its normal rate.” 

	

Why the sudden surge? Even MapQuest acknowledges it’s mostly to do with a rejection of “Lake America,” with the brand refusing to update “Lake Ontario” on its platform in the wake of a recent executive order in the US which Google Maps and more recently Apple Maps have updated their maps to show. The viral nature of that stand reminded many that MapQuest even still exists, and brought about this wave of popularity.

In a bid to keep users on its app, MapQuest confirmed that it is rapidly building out support for Android Auto – it already supports CarPlay on iPhone. Android Auto added support for third-party navigation apps a few years ago, and there are quite a few options available.

MapQuest still lags behind Google Maps and others in terms of live transit and other features, but supports turn-by-turn navigation, live traffic data, and more. MapQuest is currently owned by System1, an advertising company.

title: Apple’s Calendar app in iOS 27 has brand new design for key features
snippet: iOS 27 adds a variety of new features for popular apps like Notes, Reminders, and Calendar—and the Calendar app gets some notable design changes too. Here’s what’s new. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 adds a variety of new features for popular apps like Notes, Reminders, and Calendar—and the Calendar app gets some notable design changes too. Here’s what’s new.

iOS 27 gives Apple Calendar new design for event details view and event creation and editing screens

Apple’s Calendar app has stayed remarkably consistent over the years. The app tends to get new features less often than other popular Apple apps. And its design has changed very little over the years, even looking largely the same after last year’s Liquid Glass update.

But in iOS 27, Apple has notable design changes coming in two main areas:

Event details view

Event creation and editing

As seen in the image above, when you tap on any calendar event, the details view has gotten a revamp.

Information has been reorganized in a way that lets you view more details on-screen at a time. The addition of icons is a helpful visual cue that makes everything easier to parse. These changes, combined with smaller design updates, add up to a more modern overall feel.

iOS 27 also brings similar design updates when creating or editing events in Calendar.

As the image on the left shows, more information now fits on-screen and it’s all been reorganized and refreshed.

Icons are put to good use here, just like in the event details view. And you’ll notice headings now organize event parameters in a way that makes everything easier to navigate.

Beyond these two areas, the Calendar app also benefits from iOS 27’s systemwide enhancements to Liquid Glass. Overall, the update brings some of Calendar’s most noteworthy design changes in years.

title: Upgrade paths: Should Pixel 9 owners upgrade to Pixel 11? [Video]
snippet: We’ve seen a lot of people ask if making the jump from the Pixel 9 to a Pixel 11 is even worth it. The answer isn’t totally simple, but we’ll try our best to answer it here. Pixel 11 vs. Pixel 11 Pro: More similar than ever before [Video] more…
fullText:
We’ve seen a lot of people ask if making the jump from the Pixel 9 to a Pixel 11 is even worth it. The answer isn’t totally simple, but we’ll try our best to answer it here.

Pixel 11 vs. Pixel 11 Pro: More similar than ever before [Video]

Your 24-month cell plan might be coming to an end, so it’s timely to talk about this switch now, and we’ll do our best to help you decide which phone is right, which phone is wrong, and ultimately whether an upgrade is worthwhile.

An unchanged design

Let’s get the obvious out of the way at the start: the Pixel 9 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro are very, very similar. You could be forgiven for thinking they are the same. For anyone with a non-Pro phone, you’ll see more pronounced changes, but for all intents and purposes, the designs are almost identical across the entire device lineup.

Let’s get into the actual improvements. No matter what Pixel 9 phone you have, all Pixel 11 displays are better. Maybe not drastically so, but you get a jump up in maximum brightness of around 10% on the Pixel 9 to 11. The Pros get a 20% brightness jump at peak. This is something you probably would notice, but still not a major change. All the screens are well tuned, there’s no bezel reduction, just the same great experience, but brighter.

	

We know the design is the same, the core frame dimensions are identical, the same height, width, and thickness. The only visible change is in the camera bar shape and size. You can’t use your old cases on the new phone, so that is an annoyance. The Pixel 9 and 11 are within 1g, but the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL are almost 10 grams heavier than the 9 Pro and Pro XL. 

That could be due to the marginal battery size increases and maybe even the addition of Pixelsnap magnets, but it’s likely some internal changes that add a little extra mass, and better thermals too. Pixelsnap is great for connectivity, but a good case can mimic it pretty closely on the Pixel 9.

Similar software experience

One of the key differences between the Pixel 9 and Pixel 11 is Gemini Intelligence. It’s emblazoned all over the latest phone and adds some functionality that likely won’t come to the older devices unless Google has a change of heart.

You need to figure out if you care enough about some of the AI tools like App Automation, Rambler, the enhanced Proactive Assistant responses and replies for messaging, plus some of the other enhancements that the Pixel 10 added last year.

Some of this is merely fluff. Some are great features. Do they drastically improve your life? That remains to be seen.

Pixel 10 vs. Pixel 11: Where are the upgrades? [Video]

Even the move from Tensor G4 up to the G6 chip might not be a big enough leap for lots of people. Neither is an amazing performance beast, but they’re competent chips that handle most things you’ll throw at either phone.

Faster storage is arguably a bigger ingredient in the equation because apps will load faster, and you also get the benefit of a 256GB base model now. It was a long-overdue quality of life change that will make a bigger difference in the long term.

Frustratingly, getting less RAM on the Pixel 11 Pro or Pro XL versus the Pixel 9 Pro or Pro XL feels like a slap in the face. It’s not necessarily noticeable right now, save that you can have more apps in memory. Some of the RAM is wired for AI task control, so you’ll lose out here unless you pay more to get 16GB RAM.

The fact is, though, that the performance gap is not exactly a chasm, and Android 17 is identical here. Unless Google specifies otherwise, you’ll get all the same updates in the future too.

Quality cameras continue to impress

If you want a telephoto lens and have the Pixel 9, then yes, you might want to upgrade. The digital zoom is not as good on the base 9. It’s capped and isn’t going to get close to the action.

The other lenses are fairly similar, but know that the main sensor is slightly larger on the Pixel 11. With the default settings, it’s a toss-up.

Camera Looks are where we get some notable improvements. These are sensor-level filters that you can customize to tune your Pixel 11 camera output. No Pixel 9 will get these tools. It’s arguably the biggest change on a Pixel camera since the addition of a triple camera setup.

If you have a Pro phone, there is a better telephoto lens that lets you zoom up to 120X. Video modes get some upgrades, AI-powered Magic Capture, plus a new Creator Mode is here too.

Like basically every other head-to-head comparison, the camera improvements are more about refinement than redefining, which makes a Pixel camera so reliable.

I don’t think someone would be disappointed at what has changed, maybe underwhelmed given the two-year leap. The reality is that a Pixel camera has mostly been about consistency, which hasn’t changed.

Is now the time to upgrade from the Pixel 9 to the Pixel 11?

About upgrading: 9to5Google often gives specific product recommendations. Sometimes, we may suggest not upgrading, due to various reasons including, but not limited to: increased device cost, negligible performance gains, or environmental impact. Whether to upgrade is always your call, but our aim is to help you make as informed a decision as possible.

You don’t need us to tell you that the generational “leaps” are becoming less and less pronounced, even if you skip a few new releases.

Whether brands are holding certain functions back or other factors are at play is a topic rife among practically any industry observer right now. AI is playing a big role in the physical hardware you will buy now and for years to come.

In our eyes, there is only one key reason you should consider making the switch from a Pixel 9 to the Pixel 11, and that is if your phone is on its last legs or if you have the base 9 and want a telephoto lens. Those are the only two major reasons someone should consider the jump.

The Pixel 9 Pro and Pro XL are still fine phones. There seems to be no major or widespread issues that might cause people to be desperate to upgrade or switch away. It wasn’t the best phone on the market at launch, but, like any Pixel before, these devices tend to age better than others thanks to updates and enhancements courtesy of Google’s now-extensive support window.

If you’re even considering ditching a Pixel 9 Pro or Pro XL for the Pixel 11 lineup, think hard about what you’re actually getting. There isn’t anything on the software front that really warrants the substantial price increase. The new modem is good, but not a quantum leap. The camera improvements don’t provide exponential gains for photography or videography.

This is also true of most other pieces of tech right now. If your cell plan or contract is coming to an end imminently, maybe a cheap SIM plan could be a way to save cash at a time when smartphones are ballooning in price thanks to the constant march of AI development and the costs associated with the expansion.

The truth is that a two-generation upgrade cycle makes little sense today. You will simply get more bang for your buck by hanging on for another year. A battery replacement or repair would likely provide more value in most cases, given how little has truly changed over the past couple of years.

title: Here’s how much Apple is paying John Ternus as CEO, Tim Cook as executive chairman
snippet: In a new regulatory filing today, Apple revealed that new CEO John Ternus is receiving a pay package with $58 million in salary and target stock awards. The company also shared details on Tim Cook’s lucrative new deal as Apple’s executive chairman. more…
fullText:
In a new regulatory filing today, Apple revealed that new CEO John Ternus is receiving a pay package with $58 million in salary and target stock awards. The company also shared details on Tim Cook’s lucrative new deal as Apple’s executive chairman.

John Ternus’s new compensation

The numbers were disclosed in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission today. Ternus’s $58 million pay package includes two components:

Base salary: $3 million/year

Annual equity award: $55 million target value beginning fiscal 2027

75% ($41.25M) performance-based restricted stock units (RSUs)

25% ($13.75M) time-based RSUs

The performance shares depend on Apple’s total shareholder return compared with other S&P 500 companies. The time-based shares vest 12.5% every six months over four years.

For 2026, Ternus is also receiving prorated stock awards with a $2.5 million target value, covering the portion of fiscal 2026 he serves as CEO.

While Apple did not disclose Ternus’s previous salary in his role as senior vice president of hardware engineering, Bloomberg reports “that management level typically gets paid about $25 million annually when including stock, salary and bonuses.”

Tim Cook’s new compensation

Meanwhile, Tim Cook is receiving a pay package with a $47 million target value for fiscal 2027. This includes:

Base salary: $2 million/year, effective September 26

Fiscal 2027 equity award: $45 million target value

50% ($22.5M) performance-based

50% ($22.5M) time-based, vesting 12.5% every six months over four years

This is an unusually large pay package for an executive chairman role, signaling the value that Apple thinks Cook brings to the table here. Cook’s focus as executive chairman will see him managing Apple’s relationships with President Trump and the Chinese government.

For fiscal 2025, Cook’s total pay package as CEO was $74,294,811. That number, however, includes things not factored into today’s SEC filing. Those include non-equity incentive plan compensation, retirement plans, vacation days, personal security expenses, and more. Cook’s salary and stock awards totaled roughly $60.5 million for 2025.

title: Syncing Hue lights to your TV now starts at $120; Nanoleaf integration too
snippet: Syncing your Philips Hue lights to your TV display used to be a rather expensive undertaking, at $385 for the company’s Sync Box 8K. A couple of new products now bring that cost down to as little as $120. Additionally, you can now integrate Nanoleaf wall panels into your Philips Hue ecosystem thanks to a new $40 Wall Light Module … more…
fullText:
Syncing your Philips Hue lights to your TV display used to be a rather expensive undertaking, at $385 for the company’s Sync Box 8K. A couple of new products now bring that cost down to as little as $120.

Additionally, you can now integrate Nanoleaf wall panels into your Philips Hue ecosystem thanks to a new $40 Wall Light Module … 

Syncing Hue lights to your TV

Synchronizing your Philips Hue lights to your TV display can create an extremely immersive experience for anything from movies to games.

The company’s Sync Box 8K uses HDMI signals to detect the colors displayed on your TV screen and then adjusts all of the Hue lighting in the same room to match in real time. At almost $400, however, it’s an expensive option, and the bundles with Gradient Light Strips can reach over $650 for the largest TVs.

The company is now offering two more affordable options:

Sync Box 4K, which also uses an HDMI signal: $150

Play Screen Sync, which uses a camera: $120

HDMI syncing is the more accurate approach, and the new 4K model reduces costs by reducing support from four HDMI feeds to just one. The maximum supported resolution is 4K at 60Hz. 

The Play Screen Sync supports whatever is being displayed, but the color matching accuracy is compromised. There are already third-party products from companies like Govee using this approach.

Nanoleaf integration

The Verge spotted that a new Wall Light Module has been jointly launched by Philips and Nanoleaf. The $40 box makes any Nanoleaf product appear to be a Philips Hue device.

While Nanoleaf products already have HomeKit support, adding Hue compatibility can be useful for third-party apps which offer more flexibility with things like animated scenes and music syncing.

title: Orbitals Review: The Perfect Couples Co-op Game for the Switch 2
snippet: Developer Shapefarm’s debut adventure doesn’t ever really break away from its classic anime inspirations, but that might just work in its favor.
fullText:
Developer Shapefarm’s debut release is more than just a stellar couch co-op adventure: Orbitals is a celebration of vintage anime that wears its inspirations on its sleeve. It’s Cowboy Bebop, Evangelion and Sailor Moon stuffed into a high-concept sci-fi story, with lovingly crafted animated cutscenes to boot. And while Orbitals never truly breaks away from these visual touchstones to blossom into a stand-alone masterpiece, it’s aping so many nearly perfect hits that the sugary nostalgia will probably be enough to keep you satiated during the game’s short playtime.

The elephant in the room is Hazelight Studios’ string of award-winning hits, like It Takes Two and Split Fiction, which have come to define the couch co-op space over the past 10 years. It’s nearly impossible not to compare similar games to Hazelight’s output, even if that seems unfair to new studios just entering the genre.

But Orbitals holds up against the best of the best — probably in no small part because its development team is helmed by ex-Hazelight talent. Orbitals Game Director Jakob Lundgren previously told Polygon that the game would integrate a lot of the Hazelight DNA, but I actually think it positively iterates on that award-winning formula in many ways.

I spent a lot of time standing around and holding down a single button to help out my partner in It Takes Two and Split Fiction. By contrast, Orbitals ensures both players are always zooming through its challenges together, making meaningful contributions to platforming sections or puzzles without lingering too long in one place.

In Orbitals, players step into the role of young space colonists, Maki and Omura, who have spent their entire lives in a stranded space colony ravaged by a mysterious radiation storm. The only thing keeping the folks on the station alive are high-tech respawn machines, named IMs, but the danger is closing in. In order to save their found family (and potentially help everyone escape the wreckage), Maki and Omura travel into the farthest reaches of space to scavenge what they need to survive.

Studio Massket’s animated cutscenes make Orbitals much more charming than other genre fare.Shapefarm

The ’80s anime style does the heavy lifting for a by-the-numbers narrative

Despite its high-concept sci-fi premise, Orbitals’ story and its characters aren’t anything to write home about — it’s easy to see that they’re loving homages to popular anime series.

The IM respawn machines that bring the main characters back to life time and time again evoke some of Evangelion’s existential horror, though the game doesn’t delve into the implications that much. The spaceships are grimy, industrial and totally Bebop. Main character Maki acts (and looks) a bit like a magical girl, while her partner Omura is intelligent, a bit nerdy and way too prideful, like an endearing mix of Ranma and Spike Spiegel. 

It’s regrettable that none of these pieces ever feel like they successfully iterate on those beloved archetypes; the game just copies the best odds and ends from other stories and pastes them piecemeal into this new setting. Orbitals fondly reminisces on the titans of animation yesteryear, and that nostalgia goes far. But most of the game’s narrative beats feel formulaic (and not in a good way). It took me an entire play session to really start engaging with the story; I’m not sure my girlfriend ever fully emotionally engaged with the world at all.

Where It Takes Two and Split Fiction do manage to edge out Orbitals is level design: Hazelight’s best games have players jumping from world to world. Being shrunk down to explore a snow globe is a memorable experience, doubly so when that’s followed up by a perilous journey through an oversize garden. Orbitals mostly offers different flavors of broken-down spaceship to rifle through, and they start blending together once you’ve gallivanted through a handful of wrecks.

That’s not to say that the environmental design in Orbitals lacks charm. The game still offers plenty of gorgeous (and dangerous) vistas to visit throughout outer space, including asteroid field mining settlements, an iced-over power plant, a crackling, lava-filled factory and more. If you end up in an unappealing locale, you can rest assured you’ll be zooming past it soon: Orbitals is short enough that no level overstays its welcome.

The art direction and loving details baked into Orbitals’ DNA are what really hooked my partner and me, and I have no doubt that the little discoveries around every corner will be enjoyable for most players.

If you ever tire of the main story or need a break from the platforming levels, you can divert your attention to the main characters’ lovable purple cat, the little Studio Ghibli-inspired alien dudes scattered throughout the world or some seriously engaging unlockable minigames. (The best minigame is a versus mode akin to Space War, where you try to blow each other up with blasters that have absurd recoil.)

Even when puzzles leave you standing still, Orbitals necessitates a compelling level of coordination between partners.Shapefarm

Puzzles are challenging — and might be frustrating for some

I’m sitting on the fence about whether I should recommend Orbitals to a couple that never quite finished It Takes Two, Split Fiction or any other couch co-op platforming game. Unlike Hazelight’s impressive but lengthy titles, Orbitals is a bite-sized adventure, completable in around three play sessions, making for an easier commitment. But I know other couples that have struggled with the platforming in similar co-op games and drop them when a level gets too frustrating — and Orbitals features some surprisingly difficult coordinated movement challenges.

I personally enjoyed Orbitals’ brand of kinetic puzzling, which felt more active and less handhold-y than many levels in Hazelight games. My least favorite part of couch co-op games is when one player needs to stop engaging with play for the other to progress. If I’m standing on a button, pulling a lever or hanging around doing something similar, I’m probably not having much fun.

Orbitals has only a few instances in where you’ll completely stop to wait for your partner; while some doors and button presses require both players to operate them at the same time, that’s about it.

Even when you’re separated, the game keeps partners constantly engaged with one another. My girlfriend and I used lasers, water guns, jump packs and other cool gadgets to create new platforms for each other, clear out hazards like lava or forge paths in other creative ways. Orbitals forced us to pause and discuss how to time certain maneuvers, which was novel and fun. In the game’s toughest challenge, I had to match my partner’s movement tempo to send platforms back and forth across a side-scrolling screen while a nasty spirit clambered toward us.

I don’t anticipate longtime gamers to struggle with Orbitals, but the level of mechanical challenge feels a little bit higher than other genre fare. The game has many puzzles that require you to execute precision platforming in tandem with your partner, which might be frustrating for novice gamers.

While that could be a blocker for some folks, the game’s handcrafted anime art style makes it approachable, nonetheless. Orbitals is oozing with personality and constantly benefits from the attention to small details like character emotes. (Get ready to spam Omura’s wiggly dance.) And even if you completely bounce off of everything else, Orbitals is worth the upfront payment to experience Studio Massket’s beautiful ’80s-style hand-drawn anime cutscenes.

Orbitals is out now and is exclusively available on the Switch 2 for $40.

title: Google’s next Pixel Fold reportedly adopting the same crease-less display as Apple
snippet: We’re still a few days out from the debut of Apple’s first iPhone foldable which, as many have expected for years, will have a crease-less display. According to a new report, Google’s Pixel 12 Pro Fold will be adopting the same technology as Apple’s foldable. more…
fullText:
We’re still a few days out from the debut of Apple’s first iPhone foldable which, as many have expected for years, will have a crease-less display. According to a new report, Google’s Pixel 12 Pro Fold will be adopting the same technology as Apple’s foldable.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is, as we’ve mentioned, a perfectly fine foldable. But as brands such as Oppo, Honor, and most recently Samsung have gone all-in on crease-less displays, Google’s foldable is noticeably behind. 

Review: Google’s Pixel 11 Pro Fold just barely keeps up

According to a new report, Google plans a major upgrade on the Pixel 12 Pro Fold, and they’re not the only ones. The Elec reports that Google, Oppo, and Vivo are all working with Samsung Display to adopt dual-UTG (ultra-thin glass) displays for their next-gen foldables. It’s the same tech apparently set to be used on Apple’s first iPhone foldable. 

Samsung Display and partners would be building out the display and UTG assembly to the specs of each device. This sees one UTG layer above the display, with a second layer underneath and supporting the OLED panel. Samsung achieved its crease-less display using a special titanium plate under the OLED panel, while Oppo says it filled in the area of the crease using liquid 3D printing to create an even surface along with thicker glass.

	

The report mentions that Oppo and Vivo will both have releases in the first half of 2027, while Google’s next foldable will come in the second half – probably in August, as per the usual schedule.

title: Pixel Now Playing update brings interface tweaks
snippet: The next wave of Pixel app updates is starting with Google rolling out the latest version of Now Playing with interface tweaks. more…
fullText:
The next wave of Pixel app updates is starting with Google rolling out the latest version of Now Playing with interface tweaks.

When tapping on an identified song’s three-dot button, Now Playing slides up a bottom sheet. This replaces the floating menu and is better for one-handed navigation.

You’ll see track information with side-by-side buttons for Share, Add to favorites, and Remove from history. This is followed by a button to play the song and any shortcuts specific to your connected music service.

Meanwhile, the Favorites tab now includes dates and times like the History feed. There are also icon and spacing tweaks in Now Playing Settings.

	

The redesigned Now Playing launched in March, while Google in April reintroduced the “Tap to see what’s playing” shortcut on the lockscreen.

Version 2026.08.27.x of Pixel Now Playing is widely rolling out via the Google Play Store.

This follows last month’s updates to Pixel Journal that added more tools and Screenshots (extra filter options), as well as new icons for Google Calculator, Clock, Pixel Magnifier, Recorder, and Weather.

title: Sept. 2026 Android Drop: Find Hub ‘Remembered’ list, Motion Assist, & Keep in Google Messages
snippet: Google today is rolling out the September 2026 Android Drop with a number of major features. more…
fullText:
Google today is rolling out the September 2026 Android Drop with a number of major features.

Find Hub Remembered

Find Hub and Gemini can now keep track of things that don’t have a tracker tag on them. You can now tell “Gemini to remember where you placed important items.” For example, “Hey Google, remember in Find Hub that I put my passport in my bedroom drawer,” with the ability to add a photo. 

The location will be saved to a new “Remembered” tab in the Find Hub app. You can also ask Gemini for its location with a voice command. This is rolling out on Android 16+.

Motion Assist

Motion Assist on Android 17+ will help reduce motion sickness with a subtle bubble overlay on your screen that moves with the vehicle. This is “designed to help bridge the gap between what your eyes see and the movement of your ride.”

	

You can customize the color, shape, and opacity. There’s also an option to have the color and shape change every few seconds.

Android can enable Motion Assist automatically when movement in a car, bus, or train is detected, while there’s also a Quick Settings Tile shortcut.

Gemini Live Guided Vision

Gemini Live is adding Guided Vision to offer verbal “descriptions of what’s in front of you.” Use cases include “reading fine print on a food label, ordering from a menu in a low-lit restaurant, or locating household objects.”

If your camera isn’t lined up, voice feedback will guide you to reframe, pan across a space, or center an object so you get the answers you need. 

Guided Vision is available as an Accessibility shortcut or via the TalkBack menu. This is “coming soon to phones running Android 9+ in countries where Gemini is available.”

Google Messages Keep integration

Following the wide rollout of Chat themes, Google Messages is adding Google Keep integration. This lets you “share and update grocery lists or vacation notes right inside your chat.”

A “Create list” suggestion and ‘plus’ menu shortcut will bring up a sheet that lets you start creating. Once done, the list will appear inline as a shared note. This integration is rolling out starting today.

snippet: Apple TV kicks off its big fall lineup this week with Mayday, a new Ryan Reynolds film that’s part buddy comedy, part action spy thriller. And the first reviews say the movie’s a winner. more…
fullText:
Apple TV kicks off its big fall lineup this week with Mayday, a new Ryan Reynolds film that’s part buddy comedy, part action spy thriller. And the first reviews say the movie’s a winner.

Mayday reviews praise the film’s action, humor, and lead duo’s chemistry

Apple TV is best known for its shows, and has great ones airing now like Ted Lasso and sci-fi hits Dark Matter and Silo. But movies on Apple TV are on the rise too.

Joining the 15 free classic movies just added for subscribers, Apple has several high-profile original films premiering soon—and Mayday is first up.

Mayday premieres this Friday, September 4 on Apple TV (watch here).

The film stars Ryan Reynolds and Kenneth Branagh and hails from John Francis Daley and Jonathan Goldstein. That’s the duo behind Game Night, Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves, and co-writers of Horrible Bosses.

Reviews for Mayday just dropped, and they’re overwhelmingly positive. Here are some excerpts:

JoBlo: “Mayday is easily the best movie not hitting the big screen this year and one of the best streaming-only releases I can think of.”

Empire: “When you hear the words ‘buddy-comedy action movie starring Ryan Reynolds’, you probably feel like you have a good idea of what to expect — some slick fights, endless witty quips, and a reasonably entertaining time. Mayday delivers on all of that, and a little bit more.”

The Hollywood Reporter: “the popcorn film proves an entertaining diversion, thanks to the mismatched-buddy comic chemistry of the two leads. It makes you hope for the hinted-at sequel”

Many reviews mention how Mayday feels like it could have—and perhaps should have—gotten a theatrical release. 

The well-executed action sequences, charming humor, and Reynolds’ lead performance all add up to the kind of movie that could have been a hit summer blockbuster in years past.

In any case, Apple TV subscribers will get to stream it for free starting this week.

title: iOS 27 basically turns your iPhone and AirPods into an Apple Watch at the gym
snippet: GymKit has been one of Apple Watch’s smartest fitness features since it launched in 2017. Tap your watch to compatible gym equipment, and Apple Watch shares your heart rate while the machine sends back metrics like distance, incline, pace, and calories. With iOS 27, Apple is expanding that idea beyond Apple Watch. I tested the new GymKit on iPhone and AirPods Pro 3 experience with a GymKit-compatible treadmill. It basically gives you the Apple Watch GymKit workout tracking experience, just without the watch. This could be useful in a lot of scenarios. more…
fullText:
GymKit has been one of Apple Watch’s smartest fitness features since it launched in 2017. Tap your watch to compatible gym equipment, and Apple Watch shares your heart rate while the machine sends back metrics like distance, incline, pace, and calories.

With iOS 27, Apple is expanding that idea beyond Apple Watch. I tested the new GymKit on iPhone and AirPods Pro 3 experience with a GymKit-compatible treadmill. It basically gives you the Apple Watch GymKit workout tracking experience, just without the watch. This could be useful in a lot of scenarios.

GymKit, no Apple Watch required

The setup is simple. I tapped my iPhone to the treadmill, picked Indoor Walk (Indoor Run is also offered), and started the workout from the treadmill. With GymKit, workout data is stored privately on iPhone and removed from the equipment.

Once the workout started, the treadmill received heart-rate data from AirPods Pro 3. Meanwhile, the Fitness app on iPhone received the treadmill’s distance, pace, incline, and calorie data. Treadmills know details that an iPhone and AirPods can’t know on their own, especially incline and precise belt distance.

As a side note: Apple Watch has more accurate treadmill workout tracking as part of watchOS 27. GymKit remains the gold standard for accurate data, though.

GymKit also avoids two awkward gym habits. You don’t need to hold the treadmill’s metal heart-rate contacts while jogging. You also do not need to wear a Bluetooth heart-rate strap.

AirPods Pro 3 become the heart-rate source (and likely your podcast or music audio source as well). iPhone becomes the workout computer, which you can monitor during your workout. And the treadmill fills in the machine data while providing the surface for walking or running.

iPhone and AirPods have become more like an Apple Watch

Apple has been moving more fitness features onto iPhone for years. iOS first made the Fitness app useful without Apple Watch as Apple Fitness+ leaned into iPhone as an entry point. AirPods Pro 3 pushed that further as the first AirPods with heart-rate tracking, after Apple tested the idea with Powerbeats Pro 2.

iOS 27 brings those pieces together. GymKit on iPhone shouldn’t replace Apple Watch for people who wear one every day. Instead, it’s a great backup when your Apple Watch is dead, charging, or left at home.

It also gives iPhone and AirPods users a taste of the Apple Watch experience, which could attract future Apple Watch customers.

In testing with iOS 27 beta 1, my Exercise ring didn’t update as I worked out without wearing Apple Watch. But after I put my watch back on, the Exercise ring caught up, and the workout appeared in Fitness with the right data.

My sample 16-minute treadmill walk showed 0.66 miles, 65 active calories, 97 total calories, 32 feet of elevation gain, and a 115 BPM average heart rate, just like if I’d worn an Apple Watch.

If I tried to use GymKit on iPhone without AirPods, the iPhone disconnected when the workout started because it had no heart-rate source. If I tried to start GymKit from iPhone while wearing Apple Watch, iOS pointed me back to the Workout app on Apple Watch instead, though you can continue without using the watch.

AirPods heart-rate permission also matters. You can manage it in Settings under your AirPods settings and privacy options. I had turned it off, mostly as a theoretical battery-saving move, but this test convinced me to turn it back on. AirPods Pro 3 can also work with Apple Watch to provide the best available heart-rate data.

GymKit on iPhone with AirPods is a great addition to Apple’s Fitness ecosystem

GymKit on iPhone is one of those iOS 27 features that sounds small until it solves a real problem. If Apple Watch is your default workout tracker, it probably stays that way.

But if your watch dies or you forget it at home, iPhone plus AirPods Pro 3 can now log a treadmill workout with real heart-rate data and real treadmill metrics. That’s a neat upgrade, and it makes Apple’s broader Fitness strategy feel more complete.

title: Galaxy Z Fold 8 is so popular that Samsung is stealing parts from next year’s phones just to make more
snippet: Samsung has a hit on its hands with the Galaxy Z Fold 8, to the point where the company is taking parts production from its 2027 smartphones just to meet demand for the foldable. more…
fullText:
Samsung has a hit on its hands with the Galaxy Z Fold 8, to the point where the company is taking parts production from its 2027 smartphones just to meet demand for the foldable.

ZDNet Korea reports that Samsung has run into a wall when it comes to boosting Galaxy Z Fold 8 production, with demand for the foldable far outpacing initial supply. Shipping delays were seen immediately after launch, and Samsung even set out to produce one million more units. 

The problem Samsung has run into, the report brings out, is around Display Driver ICs (DDIs). This specific part is built by a Taiwan-based semiconductor foundry, UMC, on a 22nm process with the partner having “reached its limit” around building these parts. As a result, Samsung is prioritizing DDI volume that was already secured for 2027 products and shifting that to boosting production of the Galaxy Z Fold 8.

Samsung isn’t directly using parts designed for other devices here, though, as the DDI is built specifically for each individual phone model. It’s the production of these parts that is being shifted around, which is still a major change on Samsung’s part. Samsung has also requested a “super hot run” – i.e. “express service” – for the Fold 8’s DDIs in order to meet demand. 

	

This comes as the Fold 8 is partially out of stock on Samsung.com in the US, and the foldable continues to contribute to a rapidly growing foldable market. Omdia this week reports that foldable shipments will double by 2028 to the tune of around 36 million units.

title: iOS 27 gives Apple Pay its best upgrade in years with redesign
snippet: iOS 27 introduces several improvements for Apple Pay, including a fully overhauled checkout flow that’s the service’s best upgrade in years. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 introduces several improvements for Apple Pay, including a fully overhauled checkout flow that’s the service’s best upgrade in years.

New design for Apple Pay checkout screen in iOS 27 is better in every way

Apple Pay checkout screen: new (left) vs old (right) 

Apple Pay has become one of the most popular payment methods in the world. It’s so universally available that even Walmart finally gave in and added support.

And with its popularity, any significant change Apple implements could be risky—especially a design change like iOS 27 brings.

Apple Pay has a new design in iOS 27 when checking out in apps or on the web. And I’m happy to report it’s a fantastic upgrade that’s better in every way.

The old checkout design had a couple main faults:

Switching cards wasn’t intuitive

Onscreen data wasn’t easy to parse at a glance

Despite years of using Apple Pay, I’ve still never gotten used to the historic method for switching cards. I always tap near the top where the active card is displayed, only to load the address screen and have to go back to find the actual card selection menu.

iOS 27 fixes that. When you first open the checkout interface, you’ll see additional cards on either side of your default card, indicating you can swipe between them to switch. It’s quick, easy, and far more intuitive.

Additionally, iOS 27 shows more information onscreen at once, and uses colorful icons to denote relevant info like shipping method and address, billing address, and more.

The redesign makes it much easier to verify everything is accurate and as it should be. Then you can quickly double click to pay with the assurance there are no mistakes.

Changing the design for something used by millions, and with real-world consequences for errors, is a tall task. But in my opinion, Apple has done a fantastic job with iOS 27’s Apple Pay revamp.

title: Gemini overlay gets bubble minimization and multitasking on Android
snippet: The Gemini overlay on Android now has a multitasking option that gives you a floating bubble shortcut when you Minimize. more…
fullText:
The Gemini overlay on Android now has a multitasking option that gives you a floating bubble shortcut when you Minimize.

The Gemini overlay now shows a “Minimize” button above the container. It’s centered immediately after you enter a prompt, while the pill-shaped container appears at the right after the response.

This collapses the overlay into a bubble with the spark logo. Google explains how: “Gemini is still available while you multitask. Tap to expand. Drag to move or dismiss.”

That said, the Gemini bubble is fixed to one of six positions and cannot be placed anywhere. Additionally, a bug appears to reset the bubble to the bottom-right corner after every minimization.

	

After the response has loaded, you can tap outside the sheet to get back the bubble. Using the system back gesture will close the entire overlay, while you can also drag to dismiss.

This shortcut is a bit faster than opening the Gemini app and then the side panel to return to a conversation. Another way to use it is asking a question and then minimizing to do something else instead of having to wait for the response. 

Alternatively, you could use Android 17’s system Bubble option with the Gemini app for a richer experience.

The Minimize button and Gemini bubble are widely rolling out on Android today.

title: New profile of John Ternus offers insight into life and reputation of Apple CEO
snippet: John Ternus became Apple’s new CEO this week, and today the Financial Times published a profile that offers fresh insights into Ternus’s life and reputation among Apple employees and partners. more…
fullText:
John Ternus became Apple’s new CEO this week, and today the Financial Times published a profile that offers fresh insights into Ternus’s life and reputation among Apple employees and partners.

Latest John Ternus profile has fresh details on Apple’s new CEO

John Ternus is Apple’s new CEO, stepping into the role just days ago as Tim Cook transitioned to Executive Chair.

9to5Mac Editor-in-Chief Chance Miller has a great rundown here of what we know about Ternus, including his education, early career, public statements, and more.

But a new profile published today at the Financial Times adds fresh details and insights to the story.

Regarding Ternus’s reputation inside Apple, it says he “is known within the company for being both highly competent and unshowy.” A key Apple supply partner echoes this:

“It was very obvious from the earliest days that John was super-talented,” says Wendell Weeks, chief executive of longtime Apple glass supplier Corning, who started working with him during the development of the iPad nearly two decades ago. Weeks describes Ternus as a humble “good guy” but adds that his hobby of racing cars might give an insight into another side of his character. “There are not many non-passionate people that drive race cars…but at the same time, you have to be wicked calm and really dedicated to excellence if you’re good at it. And John is good at it.”

One former Apple executive did tell FT that Ternus is “relatively unknown outside the hardware organisation” at the company. It’s unclear how recently that executive was at Apple, however, as Ternus’s presence internally seems to have been elevated in the past year.

Tim Cook has said that Apple “really wanted this transition to be the best.” And per one anecdote from the profile, it seems like it’s been received that way internally.

the company is celebrating what appears to be a smooth handover. A party for Ternus at Apple Park on Tuesday included DJing from Apple Music’s creative director Zane Lowe. But not everyone was there. One employee said they were already so acclimatised to the change in CEO that they did not feel the need to attend.

Beyond these insights, FT does add a few key tidbits about Ternus’s otherwise very private personal life. The profile says he is married, has children, and was born and raised in California.

title: New iPhone Ultra details arrive for specs, multitasking, launch timing, more
snippet: Next week, the iPhone Ultra will be unveiled at Apple’s September event, and today a new Tom’s Guide interview with Mark Gurman reveals several fresh details on what to expect from specs, software, launch timing, and more. more…
fullText:
Next week, the iPhone Ultra will be unveiled at Apple’s September event, and today a new Tom’s Guide interview with Mark Gurman reveals several fresh details on what to expect from specs, software, launch timing, and more.

Here’s what’s coming with iPhone Ultra, per Mark Gurman

One week out from iPhone Ultra’s introduction, there are still new leaks arriving. Today in a new interview with Tom’s Guide, Mark Gurman shared a variety of tidbits—including some details not reported before.

MagSafe, for example, has been a recent question mark for iPhone Ultra. But Gurman was quick to say MagSafe won’t be absent. “MagSafe is there. Yeah, all indications that I’ve heard is that MagSafe is in for this foldable phone.”

When asked about specs for the iPhone Ultra, Gurman mentions:

5.5-inch cover display and 7.8-inch inner display

“Latest Apple Pro chip and latest Apple modem”

He also talks about two key features: the rumored “crease-less” display and liquid metal hinge. He says the crease isn’t entirely gone, but it’s comparable to the new Samsung foldables and might be even better thanks to the more durable hinge.

On the note of the hinge and durability, he adds:

The spec for Apple was to make the foldable phone as durable or at least close to it as any other iPhone. And that’s one of the things that they’ve spent a lot of time working on is the durability.

Multitasking was another key area addressed in the interview. Gurman previously reported that iOS 27 will enable iPad-like app layouts and side-by-side app multitasking. Today he adds that drag and drop will be supported between multiple on-screen apps, so you can quickly move data from one app to another.

Gurman also comments on launch timing, with encouraging news on that front:

I would be very surprised if the foldable phone did not come out at the same time as the new Pro phones, or very close to it. So either on the same launch date—a dual launch—or coming out within weeks later. This idea of a late October, a November launch, massive delays, supply chain issues, I don’t believe to be the case.

Finally, when asked about pricing, Gurman reiterates the same $2,000+ starting price expectation that he’s shared before.

title: New Apple CEO John Ternus now has his own X account
snippet: The new Apple CEO has just launched their social media presence on X, with the handle @johnternus. His bio is simply ‘ CEO’, and his first post simply reads ‘hello’. Today is Ternus’s first official day in the top job, with outgoing Tim Cook moving to an Executive Chair role. more…
fullText:
The new Apple CEO has just launched their social media presence on X, with the handle @johnternus. His bio is simply ‘ CEO’, and his first post simply reads ‘hello’.

Today is Ternus’s first official day in the top job, with outgoing Tim Cook moving to an Executive Chair role.

Apple’s relationship with social media, in general, is intriguing. As a company, Apple maintains the @apple account on X, but does not post content other than running sponsored ads. However, executives like former CEO Tim Cook and SVP Marketing Greg Jozwiak do have public-facing profiles. 

We don’t know yet what kind of content Ternus will post on X, but we can assume it will be similar to how Cook’s account was managed. That includes posts announcing new products, and sporadic statements on various company initiatives. 

We can expect the Ternus account to be very busy come next Wednesday, when Apple hosts its big fall product announcement event including the launch of new iPhones and Apple Watches.

Ternus has risen to the CEO role following a five year stint as SVP of Hardware Engineering, and a twenty-five year career at Apple in general. He is seen as a more product-oriented CEO than the outgoing operations-mastermind Cook.

title: Sony’s new ULT Tower party speakers start at $450
snippet: Sony has announced new additions to its ULT Tower party speaker lineup, now offering options that are much more affordable. more…
fullText:
Sony has announced new additions to its ULT Tower party speaker lineup, now offering options that are much more affordable.

The Sony ULT Tower collection kicked off back in 2024 with a pricey but powerful $1,200 speaker. The ULT Tower 9 launched earlier this year with a smaller, but still pricey $900 package. These speakers are designed with parties in mind, delivering music on a much larger scale than a traditional Bluetooth speaker.

Now, Sony is expanding the lineup.

Three new Sony ULT Tower party speakers are launching in September, starting with the most affordable of the bunch, the ULT Tower 5. This is the most compact of the bunch – it’s not exactly small – but Sony says it still delivers “impressive bass and sound pressure.” Like the rest of the lineup, it also features four sound profiles, including: 

	

ULT1: Enhances deep bass for a rich, low-frequency sound that makes your heart tremble.

ULT2: Boosts even greater power, delivering body-shaking bass and strong sound pressure.

FLAT: Reproduces music exactly as intended, delivering a true-to-source listening experience.

LIVE: Recreates the spacious feel of a live performance while preserving vocal clarity.

ULT Tower 5 starts at $450, with the whole lineup on Sony’s website, Amazon, and more.

The whole lineup also supports wireless audio alongside XLR, USB, and Line inputs, as well as having a microphone input too. Multiple speakers can also be set up in a stereo pair.

Meanwhile, ULT Tower 7 offers more power and volume, as well as adding 360-degree audio at $650.

ULT Tower Max is the last option debuting this month, jumping up to the top of the lineup at $1,500. This monstrous party speaker has three woofers (two front and one back-facing) as well as four tweeters, 360-degree sound, and “a high-powered amplifier.”

title: Lenovo IdeaPad Vibe is a MacBook Neo competitor starting at $699
snippet: Lenovo is taking on the MacBook Neo with a colorful new laptop – the IdeaPad Vibe. more…
fullText:
Lenovo is taking on the MacBook Neo with a colorful new laptop – the IdeaPad Vibe.

Announced at Lenovo Innovation World ahead of IFA, the Lenovo IdeaPad Vibe is squarely aimed at Apple’s most affordable and incredibly popular MacBook Neo, and it puts up a good fight on paper. The laptop can be outfitted with either a 14-inch or 15-inch OLED display and measures in at 14.9mm thick and from 2.87lbs. Thicker and bigger than Apple’s laptop, but not all that much heavier, at least in its starting weight. Lenovo says the Vibe will be available in both plastic and metal variations.

Metal
Plastic

It sure looks the part, though, with Lenovo teaming up with Pantone to offer 7 different color options for the IdeaPad Vibe including:

Dreamy Violet: a muted violet shade layered with inviting depth that inspires serenity, bringing a sense of comfort wherever it goes.

Spicy Gold: A rich golden yellow that blends warmth and energy, creating a confident, welcoming feeling.

Zen Green: A nature inspired green hue that evokes a sense of balance, harmony, and encourages a slower pace.

Chill Blue: An icy blue with a crisp modern vibe that stimulates refreshing clarity and an effortless fresh start energy.

Radiant Coral: Warm and uplifting with an optimistic orange boost that brings friendliness and positivity wherever it goes.

Moody Blue: Expressing credibility and confidence, a deep blue hue conveying refined elegance.

Lowkey Grey: A timeless grey projecting strength, stability, and understated sophistication.

The keyboard also features interchangeable keycaps so you can customize the look with some fun color combinations.

	

These are all metal versions

Pretty colors only matter so much, though, and Lenovo has stacked this laptop with a pretty enticing setup. You get a pair of USB-A ports, an HDMI port, two USB-C ports, a headphone jack, and even a microSD card reader. There’s a 5MP webcam (with physical privacy cover), an optional keyboard backlight, and an optional touchscreen on the 15-inch size.

But what’s under the hood?

You can pick between an AMD Ryzen AI 400 chip or a Qualcomm Snapdragon X chip. The AMD model supports up to 32GB of RAM which can be upgraded by the end user. Configurations also include up to 1TB of storage, also upgradable and featuring dual slots. The Snapdragon version supports up to 24GB of RAM and, while the storage is still upgradable, the RAM is not. Lenovo says to also expect an Intel version in the future.

The Lenovo IdeaPad Vibe is launching in two initial waves. AMD models will be available in October, with Snapdragon to follow in November. Both will start at $699.99, matching the price of the MacBook Neo since Apple’s RAM-induced price hike. 

Meanwhile, Lenovo is also introducing the IdeaCentre AIO I which is an all-in-one desktop computer with a 24-inch or 27-inch display, similar colors to the Vibe, and a price starting at $939. It will also be available starting in November.

title: Brydge announces color-matched keyboards for the entry-level iPad
snippet: Brydge, the Apple accessory company that came back from the dead back in 2023, has just announced a new set of colour-matched keyboards for the entry-level iPad. fullText:
Brydge, the Apple accessory company that came back from the dead back in 2023, has just announced a new set of colour-matched keyboards for the entry-level iPad.

While Apple offers the iPad itself in a choice of four colours, the Magic Keyboard for it is only available in white. That’s what prompted Brydge to launch its latest lineup … 

The 11-inch base model iPad is available in a choice of silver, blue, pink, and yellow. Brydge is now offering what it describes as a premium aluminium keyboard to match each of the four colours.

The idea is simple: you chose your favorite iPad color. Now your keyboard can match it. Most aluminum iPad keyboards are offered in traditional neutral finishes. Brydge 11.0 takes a different approach, using color-matched anodized aluminum designed to match the iPad’s own Blue, Pink, Yellow and Silver finishes […] creating a setup that looks like it belongs together, rather than an iPad with a keyboard simply added on.

The company says that it offers the build quality and features Brydge products are known for. This includes  a solid aluminium construction, a full-size backlit keyboard with 1.3mm of travel, an all-glass multi-touch trackpad supporting all iPadOS gestures, and strong magnets to hold the iPad in place. Bluetooth automatically reconnects when the case is opened.

Battery life is said to be up to three months without the backlight and a total of 40 hours’ use with the backlight on. It is recharged via USB-C.

Known as the Brydge 11.0, the keyboard is compatible with the iPad (10th generation) and iPad (A16), and costs $159. This compares to $249 for Apple’s Magic Keyboard Folio. The lineup is set to go on sale on the company’s website and official Amazon store around the middle of the month.

title: When is Apple releasing new AirPods?
snippet: Apple’s AirPods lineup is stronger than ever, but there are already rumors about what’s coming next. Here’s everything we know so far about when Apple will release new AirPods. more…
fullText:
Apple’s AirPods lineup is stronger than ever, but there are already rumors about what’s coming next. Here’s everything we know so far about when Apple will release new AirPods.

Apple’s current AirPods lineup

Here is Apple’s AirPods lineup as it stands today:

AirPods 4 (currently on sale for $99)

AirPods 4 with Active Noise Cancellation (currently on sale for $149)

AirPods Pro 3 (currently on sale for $99)

AirPods Max 2 (currently on sale for $479)

When is Apple releasing new AirPods? 

AirPods with cameras

The biggest change coming to Apple’s AirPods lineup is a new version of AirPods with built-in cameras.

This pair of AirPods will have a camera in both the left and the right earbuds. The cameras, however, aren’t designed for photo and video capture. Instead, they will be used in conjunction with Siri to provide context for the environment around you. Bloomberg has described them as “the eyes” for Siri.

For example, while looking at food ingredients, you could ask your AirPods what to make for dinner or for specific nutritional information. They might also integrate with other apps on your iPhone, such as Reminders and Maps, to provide environmental awareness features.

In terms of design, the AirPods with cameras will reportedly have longer stems than normal AirPods Pro to accommodate the cameras. There will also be a small LED light that automatically turns on when the cameras are capturing data.

The AirPods with cameras were originally slated for release in 2026. More recent reporting, however, suggests the timeline has slipped to late 2027 because of Apple Intelligence and Siri delays.

More on AirPods with cameras: 

AirPods with cameras: everything we learned this week

AirPods with cameras get their clearest leak yet

Camera-equipped AirPods reportedly won’t launch in 2026, despite demo video leak

AirPods Max

Apple just updated AirPods Max earlier this year with the H2 chip, a new high-dynamic range amplifier, improved audio quality, and more.

Last year, analyst Ming-Chi Kuo reported that Apple was working on a new AirPods Max model for 2027 that is lighter than the current design. It’s unclear whether this refresh is still on the roadmap.

AirPods 5

Apple released AirPods 4 in two different variants in November 2024, including one with Active Noise Cancellation and another without. 

Most recently, Bloomberg reported that Apple is set to announce AirPods 5 at next week’s “Surprise and shine” special event, alongside the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Ultra. 

Like AirPods 4, the new AirPods 5 are expected to come in two versions: 

with Active Noise Cancellation

without ANC

There aren’t any additional details on what new features AirPods 5 might offer. 

Wrap up: Should you buy AirPods now? 

Apple’s overall AirPods lineup is incredibly strong, especially if you can snag a pair on sale. 

That said, if you’re in the market for AirPods 4, I recommend waiting until next week to see what AirPods 5 have to offer. 

If you’re shopping for AirPods Pro 3 or AirPods Max, I think now is a great time to buy. 

AirPods Pro 3 were released last fall with a revamped in-ear fit, improved sound quality, and a built-in heart rate monitor. I think they are truly excellent. I don’t recommend waiting for AirPods with cameras right now, since those aren’t coming until sometime next year at the earliest.  

What do you think about the current state of the AirPods lineup? Are you interested in AirPods with cameras? Let us know down in the comments.

fullText:
Google morning. How many times have you written that before? I hope you had a lovely final weekend before Labor Day. This morning, I’m reading about tens of thousands of dollars’ worth of pristine Duck Hunt cartridges found in a box in Wisconsin, vigorously nodding my head along to John Oliver’s takedown of subscription bloat (but remember to subscribe to 9to5Google Pro anyway!), and wishing I had a 3D printer to create my dream storage and organization system.

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

I think it’s safe to say that Google’s decision over the weekend to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America has been met with a bit of pushback.

	

In a blog post, Google says that it generally abides by the Geographic Names Information System when it comes to how it presents names on maps, and since Executive Order 14420 “directs the Board on Geographic Names (‘BGN’) to immediately rename Lake Ontario to Lake America and to update the Geographic Names Information System to appropriately reflect the change,” it was merely following its own protocols. Google went through the same rigmarole when it renamed Gulf of Mexico to Gulf of America in February 2025.

One beneficiary of the drama has been MapQuest, the company whose rise and subsequent fall can be directly traced to Google Maps’ ascent over the past two decades. In social media posts on Friday, the company showed a cropped map of Lake Ontario with the caption, “We’re not changing it,” inspiring widespread support alongside understandable questions of “MapQuest still exists?!”

Over the weekend, the company’s Android and iOS downloads shot up 128%, bringing it to the top of their respective “maps & navigation apps” categories on both platforms, and app usage was up 50x, according to owner System1. 

As of writing, Apple has yet to make the same change to its Maps app, but it’ll likely happen any day now, particularly because the President is applying pressure, according to reports. 

Though the name change itself amounts to a minor scuffle within the larger trade war between the US and Canada, Google Maps’ enormous reach — and companies’ reliance on its APIs — means that long after the heat has died down, its effects will be felt indefinitely.

✉️ Inbox

Android 17 QPR2 Beta 4 rolling out with many Pixel bug fixes. Google’s relentless Android release cycle continues unabated, and Beta 4 appears more feature-filled than most.

Here’s everything new in Android 17 QPR2 Beta 4 [Gallery]

Android 17 QPR2 adds Status bar customization for notification, system icons

Google’s hyper-personalized ‘Dreambeans’ feed is now free to test. I’m still not sure exactly what Dreambeans is, but I know that it’s Google’s best new product name since Daydream.

Google made a cozy mobile game called ‘Froggy’s World’ & the whimsy is back. Just when you thought Froggy was going the way of the dodo, Google goes ahead and vibe-codes a Stardew Valley-like starring the titular amphibian. And who said Big Tech no longer has a sense of humor?

Google is making AI Overviews even bigger on some search queries. AI Overviews are becoming even harder to avoid, and it shows Google’s intent to keep people on Google, and not clicking away, as long as possible.

Gemini Notebook switching to compute-based usage limits, like Gemini app. Is the tool formerly known as NotebookLM so popular that Google needs to even further restrict its usage? I guess so.

Google announces ‘Expert Intelligence’ to let you add Play Books in Gemini Notebook. Gemini Notebook is becoming even more of a CliffsNotes competitor. Its new Expert Intelligence feature lets you embed participating books that you’ve purchased through Play Books into Gemini and treat them like a primary source. It’s an idea I’m curious to see authors either embrace or reject.

People are sticking the Fitbit Air to their bodies, literally, and it works [Gallery]. I kind of love this trend of seeing all the weird places people are sticking their Fitbit Airs (behave!). 

Google Nest lineup gets a price hike across nearly every camera & doorbell. The Google TV Streamer is getting a 50% price increase while Nest Cams and Doorbells are seeing hikes of between 11% and 33%. Not a great look for Google’s smart home platform.

🤝 Cc: David Imel

Welcome to a new project I’m calling Cc, where I ask interesting people in the community about what’s making them happy both inside and outside the world of tech. First up, my friend and long-time mobile journalist, David Imel.

What do you do for fun?

For fun I do landscape photography, host community events, hike, travel, play music and spend time with my friends. My most common hobby is walking. I love walking.

What is your relationship like with technology these days?

My relationship with technology is weird these days. I’ve been trying to do more things off-screen, like reading books and going to movies. I like hiking and walking because they get me off the internet. I feel that social media has been co-opted by oligarchs to make us hate each other; the more time I spend on social media, the worse I feel. Because of this, I’m trying to spend more time without any headphones in and without looking at screens, and it’s making me feel happier. I also do a lot of analog stuff like film photography and listening to records with my friends, because they feel more tangible.

What are three apps you can’t live without and why?

Pocket Casts. I’ve been using it for 16 years. It’s the longest app I’ve continuously used. I love it.

Viewfinder Preview and Second View. These are light meter and framing apps for my film photography. I use them all the time.

Moment Camera Pro II. I’ve been having a lot of fun taking photos on my phone and I shoot RAW through this app. It’s great.

What is a gadget that you love right now?

I’m loving the Fitbit Air. It’s nice to be able to use my analog watches but still get info about my health, especially since I’ve been taking my health more seriously this year.

What’s a recent book you loved?

I recently read both East of Eden and Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas.

East of Eden by John Steinbeck: This book is so well written. I love how wildly different the various characters are and the descriptions of Northern California.

Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas by Hunter S. Thompson: Just a wild fever dream of a book that is super fun and enjoyable to read.

What’s a recent album you loved?

The Place Behind the Stars by Streetlight Manifesto. Technically this album is only half out right now. It got delayed a few times and five of the songs are released so far. But this has been my favorite band since I discovered them in 2009 and new music from them is a blessing. The last album came out in 2013, so it’s been a long wait. The rest of the album is supposed to come out in mid-September. Currently, the album is called “Halfway to the Place Behind the Stars”.

Through This Fire Across From Peter Balkan by The Mountain Goats. This album came out last year and I love it. I was reminded of how much I loved it because The Mountain Goats just released a new album called “Days” and I did not like it much, but I listened to this one again and it is magical.

What’s a recent movie you loved?

Project Hail Mary because it was so lovely, especially in IMAX, but I also loved The Drama because of how divided it made people. And the performances were fantastic.

What’s something offline you do every day that brings you joy?

I go on very long walks every day. I usually average about 15,000 steps. I’ve also been bringing my guitar to the park almost every day and practicing it. But the #1 thing I’ve done every day since college is going to the local coffee shop every morning, catching up with the regulars and sipping some good coffee. I wake up early – usually around 7am, so it’s a really great little reprieve before the day starts.

Thank you, David, for being my guinea pig for this experiment.

➡️ FWD:

This section has some of our favorite stuff from around the internet. Great videos, weird memes, fun reads, recommended apps, whatever. Send us your recommendations!

The FTC and 22 US States are suing Amazon (PDF) over “secretly and systematically overcharg[ing] its approximately 1.2 million advertising customers by manipulating the ‘auctions’ that it uses to set the price of ads on its platform.” In response, Amazon says that the FTC “fundamentally misunderstands how advertisers behave” and that “there is also no harm to consumers.”

Tim Cook’s last day as Apple CEO was August 31st. He penned an emotional letter to Apple employees: “I hope you know how much I appreciate you and what an honor it has been to be your CEO.” He says of incoming CEO John Ternus: “I take enormous comfort in handing the helm to someone as brilliant and wonderful and capable as John. Few people understand what it takes to build products that change the world the way John does.” (9to5Mac)

You’ve probably heard about the proliferation of Flock cameras being deployed around the US to track everything from individuals moving around a city to car license plates. You’ve also probably heard about the similarly swift backlash from community members who are tired of being followed, harassed, and, in some cases, wrongfully arrested. The NYTimes Daily podcast summarizes the whole dystopian affair.

A massive swath of Valve’s production Steam database from 2003 to 2013 has leaked, and with it comes a veritable treasure trove of unfinished game files, including from Portal 2, Left 4 Dead 2, and CS:GO. (Ars Technica)

The harness that started it all mere months ago, OpenClaw, is back with a massive 2.0 update. While it now has dozens of competitors, including Hermes Agent (which I prefer), it’s nice to see the OG getting a spit-shine.

🎙️ Quotations

Due to rising component costs, we are adjusting the U.S. pricing of select Google Nest cameras, doorbells and Google TV streamer 4K, effective August 31. We remain committed to providing our customers with industry-leading smart home security and continuous feature updates.

– Google, on justifying its up to 50% increase in Google Nest products this week

title: Apple TV leads Emmys wins so far, with Widows Bay set for awards sweep
snippet: The prestigious television Emmy Awards began this weekend, with the winners announced for Creative Arts categories. The Primetime award ceremony is coming up on September 14th, which will include the big categories like Best Drama and Best Comedy.
